`ramennoodles` adds ramen noodles, bringing the current catalog from 934 to 935 kinds (936 gallery choices including plain). Each tile holds 22 wavy noodle strands running along u, layered from top to bottom with later strands lying over earlier ones: the center line of strand i is y = (i + 0.5)/22 + 0.085·sin(2π(k·u + phase)), with k cycling through 3, 4, 5 and the phase taken from the golden ratio (the fractional part of i × 0.618…), so the strand shapes are the same for every seed and only tone and grain change with the seed; strands have a half width of 0.026 and a round tube profile (bright along the center line, darker toward the edges with lower height and ambient occlusion), ±0.06 per-strand tone variation, and about 7% of the area shows dark broth between strands. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: there are no curled noodles, breaks, oil slicks, toppings or broth reflections; because every strand is a wave with a fixed stacking order, the pile looks fairly regular. Distance to a strand uses a first-order approximation (vertical offset over √(1 + slope²)), so strand width is slightly off where the slope is steep at the crests. Defaults are a 0.3 m nominal tile, 0.01 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `connectfourboard` adds a Connect Four board, bringing the current catalog from 935 to 936 kinds (937 gallery choices including plain). Each tile holds one 7-column × 6-row board with one extra row of base tray below: a blue panel with round holes, each hole dark (empty) or holding the first player's disc (mid tone) or the second player's disc (near-white), with an inner ring and a slightly raised rim. The position comes from simulating a legal game from the seed: the two players alternate dropping discs into random columns (the first player starts), discs stack from the bottom by gravity, and a drop that would complete four in a row is rerolled into another column; there are 18–30 moves. So every column's discs are unbroken from the bottom, the first player has either as many discs as the second or exactly one more, and nobody has completed four in a row. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: there is no real red and yellow (colors are brightness interpolated linearly between the dark and light ends, so the first player is a mid blue-gray and the second near-white); the position is a random legal one, not a played strategy, and nothing guarantees that both sides would "sensibly" have played it. `pegsolitaire` adds peg solitaire, bringing the current catalog from 937 to 938 kinds (939 gallery choices including plain). Each tile holds one 7×7 English cross board: the four 2×2 corners are solid wood with no holes, the other 33 cells are holes holding either nothing (dark) or a light round-headed wooden peg (with a highlight and a small dome). The position comes from the seed by starting at the solved end state (one peg in the center) and playing 8 random moves backwards (each reverse jump turns "peg, empty, empty" in a line into "empty, peg, peg"), so the picture — 9 pegs, or fewer if the attempt budget runs out — can always be solved to a single peg by playing the jumps forward. The board has wood grain stretched along u. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the position is guaranteed only to be solvable (it comes from reverse play), not to be the shortest solution or a representative puzzle; only the 33-hole English board is drawn, not the 37-hole French board or other variants; colors are brightness interpolated linearly between the dark and light ends, so the pegs are a pale tan rather than a specific color. `xylophonebars` adds xylophone bars, bringing the current catalog from 938 to 939 kinds (940 gallery choices including plain). Each tile holds 12 wooden bars side by side (the twelve semitones of an octave), all centered on the middle line of the tile; the first is the longest (0.9 tile) and each following bar is 2^(−1/24) ≈ 0.9715 of the previous one — a tuned bar's frequency goes as 1/length², so one equal-tempered semitone (frequency ratio 2^(1/12)) shortens it by 2^(−1/24), and twelve semitones (an octave) by 2^(−1/2). Each bar has a suspension hole 22.4% in from each end (the node positions of the first free–free bending mode), and the holes of neighboring bars are joined by a thin line (the cord); the wood grain runs along the bar and the bar tone lightens slightly from long to short on a dark felt background. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only the length ratios and node positions are drawn — bar thickness, width and cross-section (real xylophone bars are often undercut to tune the overtones) are not modeled, nor are resonator tubes; the cord is a straight line between holes and snaps back at the tile seam (from the last bar to the next tile's first bar), a deliberate discontinuity. Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile, 0.0035 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. `sliderulescale` adds slide-rule scales, bringing the current catalog from 939 to 940 kinds (941 gallery choices including plain). Each tile stacks 8 ivory logarithmic C scales, one decade spanning the whole tile width: the graduation x is drawn at u = log10(x), so 10 coincides with the 1 of the next tile and the tile repeats seamlessly. Graduations follow the usual rule — every 0.02 in [1, 2), every 0.05 in [2, 4), every 0.1 in [4, 10) — for 150 ticks at three lengths: integers (9, longest), tenths in [1, 4) and halves in [4, 10) (33 medium) and the remaining 108 shortest; each integer tick has a 3×5 dot-matrix digit 1 to 9 to its right. Each scale has a thin line along its top and bottom, the ink varies slightly in density and the paper has a fine grain. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only a single decade of the C scale is drawn — no other scales (A/B/D/CI/K/S/T/L), no cursor, no markings or lettering; digits use a 3×5 dot matrix rather than a printed typeface; the graduation rule is the common one and not a reproduction of a particular maker's model; colors are linear brightness interpolation (ivory base, near-black ink) and do not represent real material hues. `spirographrosettes` adds spirograph rosettes, bringing the current catalog from 940 to 941 kinds (942 gallery choices including plain). Each tile draws one hypotrochoid per quadrant (the curve traced by a pen at some distance from the center of a small gear rolling inside a large ring) with ring/gear radius ratios 5/3, 8/3, 7/2 and 9/4, giving 5, 8, 7 and 9 lobes (for coprime R and r the lobe count equals R); the curve closes after t has run through 2π·r/gcd(R, r). The pen distance varies with the seed and quadrant between 0.37 and 0.73 gear radii and each figure is rotated by the seed; the pen always reaches exactly the outer circle (radius 0.215 tile), so all lobe tips lie on one circle. The four quadrants use slightly different ink brightness and the paper has a fine grain. Metallic and mortar are 0.

Implementation: when the sampler is created the curves are stamped (about 108 thousand points) into a 640×640 Float32 ink-coverage mask (about 1.6 MB, one per sampler) and every sample is just a bilinear lookup; the mask resolution is fixed at 640, so above 640 px the lines are magnified by the bilinear filter and get slightly softer rather than sharper.

This is an authored schematic: only four fixed ring/gear ratios are drawn (not arbitrary R, r), the curve is a polyline of uniformly spaced t samples (9000 points per loop, not an exact distance field); colors are brightness interpolation (near-black ink on cream paper) and do not represent pen hues. Defaults are a 0.3 m nominal tile, 0.0012 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 512 to 1024; 32 is a coarse preview. This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`juliacells` adds Julia-set cells, bringing the current catalog from 941 to 942 kinds (943 gallery choices including plain). Each tile draws one filled Julia set z → z² + c per quadrant with a real c (about −0.4, −0.75, −1.0 and −1.25, each jittered by up to ±0.04 by the seed; for real c in [−2, 1/4] the set is connected and the picture is mirror symmetric in both axes). Each cell's view radius is 2, equal to the escape radius, so points on a cell border escape immediately and there is no seam between cells or at the tile repeat. The interior (points still bounded after 96 iterations) is near black; outside, the smooth escape count μ = n + 1 − log₂(ln|z| / ln 2) drives a glow 1 − exp(−μ/9) from dark to bright, and height and roughness follow the same glow. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only four real-parameter Julia sets — no Mandelbrot set and no complex c (a complex c is not mirror symmetric and would leave a seam at the tile border); the iteration cap is 96, so slowly escaping points near the boundary are drawn as interior; colors are brightness interpolation (near-black navy to warm cream) and do not represent any particular palette. Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile, 0.0035 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `weavingdraft` adds a weaving draft, bringing the current catalog from 944 to 945 kinds (946 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a 16×16-cell sheet showing the full draft for a four-shaft loom: the 12×4 block at the top left is the threading (which shaft each warp thread runs through, one mark per column, shaft 1 in the row nearest the drawdown), the 4×4 block at the top right is the tie-up (which shafts each treadle lifts), the 12×4 block at the bottom right is the treadling (which treadle is pressed for each weft pass, one mark per row), and the 12×12 block at the bottom left is the drawdown they determine: a dark cell means that warp thread floats on top for that pass (its shaft is lifted), a light cell means the weft is on top. Threading and treadling are chosen at random by the seed, and every treadle lifts a non-empty, non-full set of shafts (1 to 3), so the drawdown is fully fixed by the rule. Metallic and mortar are 0.

The cube is scrambled by the seed with 22 random quarter turns of the outer layers (rotating the 3D positions and normals, not random coloring), so the picture is always a legal, solvable cube state: each brightness appears on exactly 9 stickers, the six centers are six different brightnesses, each of the 12 edge pieces and 8 corner pieces appears exactly once, and no piece pairs colors from opposite faces. `knightstour` adds a knight's tour, bringing the current catalog from 946 to 947 kinds (948 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is an 8×8 chessboard of alternating light and dark squares, every square numbered 1 to 64 in 3×5 dot-matrix digits along an open knight's tour (each step an L-shaped knight move, no square visited twice), with a faint thin line joining the centers of consecutively numbered squares. The tour is found when the sampler is created by depth-first search that tries the square with the fewest onward moves first (Warnsdorff's rule), breaking ties by the seed; each attempt has a node budget (40000) and a failure restarts from another square (up to 60 attempts); the start and the route vary with the seed. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only an open route is drawn, not required to return to the start (not a closed tour); there are no pieces; where the thin line crosses digits the digits are drawn on top of it; the search is a budgeted heuristic, not exhaustive — on 600 seeds a complete 64-step route was in fact found every time (the slowest creation was about 49 ms, a one-off local measurement and not a benchmark), but that does not prove every seed succeeds; if all 60 attempts failed, the squares reached would be numbered and the rest left blank (not observed here). Colors are brightness interpolation (light/dark cream squares and near-black ink) and do not represent a real board material. `graycodediscs` adds Gray-code encoder discs, bringing the current catalog from 947 to 948 kinds (949 gallery choices including plain). Each tile has four optical rotary-encoder discs, one per quadrant, with 3, 4, 5 and 6 concentric tracks (8, 16, 32 and 64 sectors): sectors are numbered from the +u direction toward +v (clockwise on screen), and track k (counted from the outside, so the outermost is the fastest-changing bit 0) is a bright clear slot where bit k of the sector's Gray code g = s XOR (s >> 1) is 1 and a dark opaque block where it is 0, so neighboring sectors (including the last one wrapping to the first) differ in exactly one track. The rim carries thin sector tick marks, there is a dark shaft hole in the center and a mid-grey mat outside the disc. Metallic and mortar are 0.

`code39barcodes` adds Code 39 barcodes, bringing the current catalog from 948 to 949 kinds (950 gallery choices including plain). Each tile has 6 rows of barcodes, each of the form `*XXXXX*`: the start/stop character `*` around 5 characters chosen by the seed (0–9, A–Z, `-`, `.`). Every character is 9 elements (5 black bars and 4 spaces, starting with a bar) of which exactly 3 are wide (3× the narrow width) and 6 narrow; characters are separated by one narrow space, with quiet zones of at least 10 narrow units before and after. The paper is cream, the bars carry slight ink density variation and grain. Metallic and mortar are 0.

The pattern table was typed from memory and decoded back independently in the tests using the structural rule described on Wikipedia's Code 39 page (two wide bars encode a number 1–10 with the weights 1, 2, 4, 7, 0; the one wide space out of four picks one of the groups U–Z plus symbols / digits / A–J / K–T), confirming that the patterns of all 38 data characters and of the `*` delimiter follow that rule; they were not checked against a real barcode scanner or the full text of ISO/IEC 16388, and the codes were never actually scanned.

This is an authored schematic: no Code 39 check digit (the symbology does not require one), none of the symbols `$`, `/`, `+`, `%` and the space character (it can be encoded but this alphabet does not use it), no human-readable text; the wide-to-narrow ratio is fixed at 3:1 and a unit is 1/132 of the tile, so very low resolutions (such as 32) cannot resolve the narrow bars. Defaults are a 0.3 m nominal tile, 0.0012 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Each tile is an amidakuji with 8 vertical lines and 10 rung levels: at each level the seed draws rungs between neighboring lines at random (about 45% chance, never two touching rungs on one level); a row on top is numbered with the start numbers 1 to 8 and a row at the bottom shows, under each line, the start that ends there — every start walks down its line and moves across whenever it meets a rung, so the bottom row is a permutation of the top. The label bands are grey, the digits are 3×5 dot matrix, the paper cream and the ink near-black. Metallic and mortar are 0.

The longest barb (about 0.24 tile) is still shorter than the 0.25 tile from shaft to boundary, so each feather leaves a margin of at least about 0.01 tile at the boundaries, so no barbs touch across the tile seam or between the two feathers. Metallic and mortar are 0.

`dartboardsectors` adds a dartboard, bringing the current catalog from 951 to 952 kinds (953 gallery choices including plain). `quasicrystalwaves` adds quasicrystal-style waves, bringing the current catalog from 953 to 954 kinds (955 gallery choices including plain). Five plane waves cos(2π(m·x) + φ) are summed, with integer wave vectors m = (6, 0), (2, 6), (−5, 4), (−5, −4), (2, −6) that point roughly in the five directions of a regular pentagon (neighboring angles within 10° of 72°, length ratio below 1.15) and phases φ chosen by the seed; the sum S goes through the monotonic map 0.5 + 0.5·tanh(0.7·S) to the brightness (height and roughness come from the same sum), giving an approximately five-fold symmetric picture of spots and pentagram-like structures. Because the wave vectors are integers the whole pattern is exactly periodic over the tile and repeats seamlessly. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: it is a periodic approximant, not a true quasicrystal — a real one (such as a Penrose tiling) has no translational period; the five-fold symmetry here is only approximate (the angle and length errors of rounding the vectors to integers) and the pattern still repeats at a distance; there is no diffraction and no physical quasicrystal meaning; colors are brightness interpolation (near-black navy to warm cream) and do not represent a particular palette. `doubleslitfringes` adds double-slit interference fringes, bringing the current catalog from 960 to 961 kinds (962 gallery choices including plain). Each tile stacks four far-field double-slit patterns whose intensity along the horizontal is I(x) = cos²(πx/p) · sinc²(πx/(r·p)), with x the offset from the center, p = 1/16 tile the fringe period and r the slit separation divided by the slit width; the four panels use r = 2, 3, 4, 5: the fringes sit at whole multiples of p, and when the order m is a multiple of r it falls exactly on a zero of the single-slit sinc² envelope and is missing. The brightness is I^0.6, on a dark background with cream fringes and a thin dark gap between panels. The pattern is mirror symmetric about the center, so it is continuous at the tile seam and repeats seamlessly. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: it is the idealized far-field (Fraunhofer) formula, not an experimental image — no finite screen distance, finite source width or non-monochromatic blurring of the fringes, and no physical intensity units; the pattern is one-dimensional along the horizontal and merely repeated vertically; the seed only changes a very fine grain; colors are brightness (near-black blue to cream) and do not represent a particular wavelength of light. This is an authored schematic: the spiral is the Fibonacci-square approximation (quarter-circle arcs joined tangentially, with curvature jumping at the joints), not a true logarithmic spiral; the rectangle does not fill the tile and leaves blank margins, so there are gaps between the figures when the tile repeats; only seven squares (the largest 13) are drawn and it cannot be extended; the seed only changes the paper grain. `bluenoisemask` adds a blue-noise mask, bringing the current catalog from 962 to 963 kinds (964 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a 64×64 blue-noise dither mask built with the void-and-cluster algorithm (Ulichney): on a torus (edges wrapping) a Gaussian energy (σ = 1.5) finds the "tightest cluster" and the "largest void"; about 10% random initial points are relaxed to a stable pattern, then all 4096 texels are ranked 0 to 4095 with every rank used exactly once; brightness = rank ÷ 4095, so the brightness histogram is exactly flat and low-frequency energy is strongly suppressed. The mask is computed on a torus and repeats seamlessly; height rises with brightness and roughness rises slightly. Metallic and mortar are 0.

One-off local measurement (seed 0, discrete Fourier power of the 64×64 mask divided by the power expected for white noise): about 0.000 for frequencies of radius 1 to 5, about 0.003 for radius 8 to 12 and about 1.61 for radius 24 to 31 (near Nyquist); a random permutation of the same variance (white noise) gives about 1.21, 1.14 and 0.96. Creating a sampler takes about 66 ms (one-off, not a benchmark).

This is an authored product with limits: the mask size is fixed at 64×64 texels (larger would make the algorithm too slow) and it is sampled nearest-neighbour, so on a 512 px image each texel is an 8×8 px block (for texel-exact blue noise set the size to 64 or sample it with repeat in a shader); the seed only chooses the initial random points — different seeds give different masks of similar spectral quality; colors are brightness with no hue meaning. Defaults are a 0.2 m nominal tile, 0.002 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. `elementaryautomata` adds one-dimensional elementary cellular automata, bringing the current catalog from 963 to 964 kinds (965 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is 2×2 panels of 31×31 cells, each evolving one Wolfram rule from top to bottom — rule 90 top left (Sierpinski triangle), 110 top right, 150 bottom left and 184 bottom right (the traffic rule): row 0 is the middle cell plus a sparse seed-chosen scatter of about 12%, and each next row is computed from the previous one by the rule (on a ring of 31 cells, the ends wrapping). Live cells are small near-black squares, dead cells small light-grey squares, a thin line separates the panels and the paper is cream. Because the ring has 31 cells (odd), rule 90 does not die out to all zeros after a few steps the way it does with 32 cells; the pattern continues to the bottom. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only four rules, a fixed width of 31 cells and 31 rows; the ring boundary makes the pattern wrap around the left and right edges (it does not continue into the neighboring panels); the first row contains random points, so it is not the classic single-seed triangle (set seedDensity to 0 for a single seed); "an odd ring does not die out" was observed on the seeds tested here and has no mathematical proof; colors are brightness (near-black ink, light-grey grid, cream paper). `magicsquares` adds magic squares, bringing the current catalog from 966 to 967 kinds (968 gallery choices including plain). Each tile holds one magic square per quadrant: order 3 (Lo Shu), order 4 (Dürer's square), and orders 5 and 7 (the odd orders by the Siamese method: start in the middle of the top row, move up and right, and step down one row when the cell is taken); each square is rotated 0 to 3 times by the seed and possibly reflected (rotation and reflection keep the property). So the numbers of each square are exactly 1 to n² once each, and every row, column and both diagonals sum to the magic constant n(n²+1)/2 (15, 34, 65, 175). Numbers are 3×5 dot matrix (one or two digits) with grid lines and a heavier outer frame on cream paper. Metallic and mortar are 0.

`sortingnetworks` adds sorting network diagrams, bringing the current catalog from 978 to 979 kinds (980 gallery choices including plain). In each of the four quadrants of the tile an 8-wire sorting network is drawn: eight horizontal wires (0 to 7 from top to bottom) and each comparator is a bright vertical bar with a dot at each end joining the two wires it compares (the smaller value goes to the upper wire). The seed picks one of two networks per quadrant: Batcher's odd-even merge sort (19 comparators) or the bitonic sorter (24 comparators, in its all-ascending form); every comparator gets its own column, left to right in execution order. A dark blue panel with faint grain and a thin frame. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only 8 wires and two networks; to keep nested comparators from overlapping, each comparator has a column to itself (so the comparators of one layer are not drawn in a shared column as in the standard layered drawing); the test reads the comparator network back and checks with the 0-1 principle that it sorts all 256 binary inputs, but does not show that it has the fewest possible comparators. Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile, 0.003 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`primesieve` adds a prime sieve, bringing the current catalog from 979 to 980 kinds (981 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a 16×16 board of rounded squares holding 256 consecutive integers row by row, left to right and top to bottom, starting at a number the seed picks between 1 and 745. Primes are the brightest yellow squares and are raised; composites are shaded by their smallest prime factor into five grey-yellow levels (dark to bright) for 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11 or more; the number 1 (if the window contains it) is the darkest square. The primes therefore sit exactly where the sieve of Eratosthenes leaves gaps, and multiples of 2 show up as dark vertical stripes every other column. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: there are no digits on the tile, so the numbers can only be inferred from the pattern; the smallest prime factors of 11 or more share one level (11, 13, 17… are not separated); the largest start is 745, so the window goes up to 1000 (the largest smallest prime factor is 31); brightness is grayscale, not hue; primality is decided by trial division, not by implementing the sieve. Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`knockoutbracket` adds a knockout tournament bracket, bringing the current catalog from 980 to 981 kinds (982 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is the tree of a 16-team single-elimination tournament: on the left, round one is teams 1 to 16 shuffled by the seed (dot-matrix numbers, two glyphs for two digits), and to the right come the quarter-finals, semi-finals, final and champion as five columns of boxes, with the two boxes of each match joined by lines into the next column, whose box holds the winner of that match (the seed randomly picks the upper or the lower team), so every winner's number equals one of the two boxes that feed it, and the rightmost, brighter box is the champion. Light boxes, dark numbers and grey connectors on a dark blue background. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the results are entirely random and do not represent strength or a score; there are no scores, team names or dates; it is fixed at 16 teams with no byes or third-place match; the numbers are 3×5 dot matrix and a two-digit number is about 0.05 tile wide. Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`skyscraperpuzzles` adds Skyscraper puzzles, bringing the current catalog from 981 to 982 kinds (983 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is split into 2×2 solved Skyscraper puzzles of order 4, 5, 6 and 7 in reading order: the middle is an n×n grid in which each cell is the height of a building (a dot-matrix digit from 1 to n, with a slightly darker and higher base for taller buildings) and every row and column holds 1 to n once each; the ring around it holds the clues giving how many buildings can be seen looking in from that side (taller buildings hide shorter ones behind them, so only buildings taller than all before them are counted). The digits are 3×5 dot matrix on cream paper with thin grid lines and a frame. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the tile shows the solved answer with all four sides of clues (a real puzzle gives only the clues and hides the digits inside); the solutions are cyclic Latin squares with row, column and symbol permutations, so they do not cover all possible solutions; the digits 1 to n are printed in dot matrix and the order-7 cells are small (about 0.05 tile). Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. `pianoroll` adds a piano roll, bringing the current catalog from 982 to 983 kinds (984 gallery choices including plain). Each tile looks like a piano-roll editor: on the left a keyboard strip of 24 semitones (two octaves) with white keys as bright rows and black keys (C♯, D♯, F♯, G♯ and A♯ of each octave) as dark rows, and on the right a grid of 24 rows × 32 steps (with a more visible beat line every 4 steps) in which a melody is drawn as bright blue bars. The melody uses a major scale picked by the seed (one of the 12 tonics), starts on the tonic, moves one or two scale degrees at a time without repeating a pitch, with notes of 1 to 4 steps until the 32 steps are full; higher notes are brighter. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the melody is a random walk with no rhythmic or harmonic musicality; the pitch range is fixed at 24 semitones (two octaves) with the tonic in the middle-to-upper part; only a major scale is used, with no modulation, chords or rests; the keyboard strip is drawn as bright and dark rows, not as real key shapes. Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `binaryclock` adds a binary clock, bringing the current catalog from 983 to 984 kinds (985 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is split into 2×2 clock panels that show four consecutive seconds in reading order: the clock shows hh:mm:ss as six decimal digits in binary coded decimal (BCD), each digit a column of four dots whose bits from top to bottom are 8, 4, 2 and 1, bright green meaning 1 and dark meaning 0. The start time is picked by the seed anywhere in a day (00:00:00 to 23:59:59), so the last column (the units of the seconds) advances from panel to panel, and when the seconds roll over (for example at 59) the carry runs on into the minutes and hours, wrapping from 23:59:59 to 00:00:00. A thin frame surrounds each dark panel. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: it is a 24-hour clock only, with no date or milliseconds; the start time comes from the seed and the nine seeds in the tests do not necessarily include a minute or day rollover (the modulo logic for the carry is written but not covered by these seeds — see ACCEPTANCE); the dots carry no labels for their bit weights (8, 4, 2, 1). Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 512 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. `othelloboard` adds an Othello board, bringing the current catalog from 984 to 985 kinds (986 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is split into 2×2 green 8×8 boards which, in reading order, are four consecutive positions of a random game of Othello/Reversi, each the result of one more legal move after the previous one: starting from the standard opening (four discs in the centre), black first, the seed drives 14 to 32 random legal moves, and the position after them plus the three that follow are shown; a move places one new disc and flips the runs of opposing discs it brackets along the eight directions, and a player with no legal move passes. Black discs are dark, white discs bright, on a green felt board with thin grid lines in a dark wooden frame. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the game is entirely random legal moves, not a meaningful game, and the positions are not guaranteed to look like a real match (the preview often shows discs in rows or crosses); only four consecutive positions are shown and it is not marked whose turn it is; the test verifies each move's flips with an independent eight-direction ray scan but does not check that the whole game could have legally led from the opening to the first position (only the one-move steps between neighbouring positions). Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 512 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. `goboards` adds Go boards, bringing the current catalog from 985 to 986 kinds (987 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is split into 2×2 wood-grained 9×9 Go boards (thin grid lines, five star points, dark wooden frame), the four being positions of random legal games after 16, 28, 42 and 58 moves: black and white alternate, black first, each move goes on a random empty point; if it leaves an opposing group with no liberties that group is captured and removed, and if the played stone's own group would have no liberties the move is rejected and another point is tried (no suicide). Black stones are dark discs, white stones bright discs. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the game is entirely random, not a meaningful game or a life-and-death problem; only capture and the no-suicide rule are implemented — there is no ko rule, no passing, scoring or end of game; if 40 tries find no legal point the move is skipped, so a board can have fewer stones than moves; white stones use the brightest end of the colour ramp, which in this material (a single dark-to-light gradient) is cream rather than pure white. Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 512 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. `dewbeads` adds dew drops, bringing the current catalog from 986 to 987 kinds (988 gallery choices including plain). On a dark green leaf with thin slanting veins and a soft mottling lie round dew drops: the tile is split into 12×12 cells and each cell holds a drop with about 62% probability, with a radius between 0.014 and 0.028 of the tile width and a position jittered inside the cell so drops never touch each other or cross the tile edge. A drop's height is a spherical cap (highest at the centre, falling towards the edge as √(1−d²) where d is the distance from the centre over the radius) and its colour is refraction-like: bright in the middle, dark at the rim, with a small highlight towards the upper left; it is smoother than the leaf. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: a drop is just a simple spherical cap, with no real refraction or reflection and no water film or running; positions are bound to the cells, so a faint grid arrangement can still be seen; the leaf is artificial slanting veins plus noise mottling, not a real leaf; the colour is a single dark-to-light ramp (the green hue comes from the preset's dark and light ends). Defaults are a 0.3 m nominal tile, 0.008 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. `bowlingscoresheet` adds a bowling score sheet, bringing the current catalog from 987 to 988 kinds (989 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is the score sheet of four games of ten-pin bowling (one row per game, ten frames): the top right of each frame holds the roll boxes — two small boxes in frames 1 to 9 and three in frame 10 — recording each roll in order, a strike as "X", a spare as "/", a miss (0 pins) as "-" and otherwise the number of pins knocked down, 1 to 9; below them is the cumulative score in dot-matrix digits. The rolls are random from the seed (about a 30% chance of a strike or spare on each ball, otherwise any number of the pins left); the cumulative score follows the standard rules: a strike scores 10 plus the next two rolls, a spare 10 plus the next roll, otherwise the pins of the two rolls; frame 10 gives a third roll after a strike or spare, and in frames 1 to 9 a strike is written only in the right-hand box. Cream paper with grey grid lines and dark ink. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the rolls are random and not the distribution of a real bowler (strikes and spares are a fixed 30% each, so scores run high and runs of strikes are common); there are only four games and no player names, dates or title; the notation in frame 10 (for example that a ball clearing the rack after a strike is also written as X) follows common practice and was not checked against any official rulebook; the numbers are 3×5 dot matrix. Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.003 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. `hexresourceboard` adds a hexagonal resource-island board, bringing the current catalog from 988 to 989 kinds (990 gallery choices including plain). The middle of each tile holds an island of 19 hexagons (arranged 3, 4, 5, 4, 3) surrounded by dark blue sea. The hexagons use six brightness levels for six kinds of terrain, in the numbers 4, 3, 4, 4, 3 and 1 (the brightest kind occurs once, like a desert), with the seed shuffling which kind goes where; each of the 18 hexagons except the desert carries a round number token, using 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 8, 8, 9, 9, 10, 10, 11, 11, 12 once each, with the Catan rule that the two "red" numbers 6 and 8 never sit on adjacent hexagons (the seed's shuffle is retried until that holds). A token is a light disc with a dark dot-matrix number, and the sea has faint swell. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: terrain is told apart only by brightness, with no forests, pastures or other pictures, and the 6s and 8s are not drawn red (this material has a single dark-to-light ramp); the number and terrain layout follow the rules above, but the rules were implemented from memory and not checked against the official rulebook; if 400 shuffles cannot satisfy the "6 and 8 not adjacent" condition the last one is kept (the sampled seeds in the tests never needed that); there is a single island per tile with no special handling for repeating the tile. Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.005 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. `kakuropuzzle` adds a Kakuro puzzle, bringing the current catalog from 989 to 990 kinds (991 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a solved 8×8 Kakuro grid: the first row and first column are black cells, the seed adds 6 to 9 random black cells inside, and only layouts in which every run of white cells has at least two cells are kept; the white cells are filled with digits 1 to 9 so that no digit repeats within any horizontal or vertical run (a randomised backtracking fill); the black cell just before the start of each run (to its left or above it) is split by a diagonal line, with the across sum at the top right and the down sum at the bottom left (small one- or two-digit dot-matrix numbers). Cream paper and dark black cells with large dark dot-matrix digits in the white cells. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the tile shows the solved grid, while a real Kakuro shows only the clues and hides the white-cell digits; the layout comes from random black cells with only the condition that every white run is at least 2 long, so a unique solution and a good puzzle are not guaranteed; the layout search tries up to 6000 times per seed and I only checked that 209 seeds (the 9 test seeds plus 200 extra ones) found a layout; the dot-matrix digits are 3×5 and a two-digit clue is about 0.045 tile wide. Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. `hashibridges` adds a bridge puzzle (Hashiwokakero), bringing the current catalog from 990 to 991 kinds (992 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a solved bridge puzzle on a 9×9 lattice: round islands carry dot-matrix numbers 1 to 8 and are joined by horizontal or vertical single or double bridges, each island's number equals the total number of bridges attached to it (a double bridge counts 2), bridges never cross, and all islands are connected. The seed builds the layout: starting from one island, it repeatedly goes in a random direction, leaves at least one empty cell, and puts a new island there joined by a bridge (about 40% double), reaching about 15 islands (limited by the attempt count, so sometimes fewer), then adds random bridges between pairs of islands that are in line with nothing between them (about 30% of such pairs). Cream paper with faint lattice dots, islands as light discs with a thin dark ring and number. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the tile shows the solved bridges, while a real puzzle gives only the island numbers and hides the bridges; the generator guarantees connectivity and no crossings but not that this bridge arrangement is the unique solution to these numbers (real puzzles require uniqueness), and sometimes there are fewer than 15 islands; single and double bridges are close together (the two lines of a double bridge are about 0.016 tile apart). Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`slitherlinkloop` adds a Slitherlink puzzle, bringing the current catalog from 991 to 992 kinds (993 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a solved 7×7 Slitherlink board: lattice dots are small circles, one thick dark closed loop runs along the lattice lines with the cells inside it slightly darker, and the middle of every cell holds (a dot-matrix digit 0 to 3) how many of its four sides are part of the loop. The loop is the outline of a randomly grown connected region (about 55% of the cells): the seed drives the growth, and only regions whose outline has 0 or 2 edges at every lattice dot and can be walked in one lap through all loop dots (a single cycle, with no holes or blocks touching only at a corner) are accepted. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the tile shows the answer (the loop) together with the numbers of all cells, while a real puzzle gives only some numbers and hides the loop; the region comes from random growth and tends to extend from a particular corner (the preview often shows a shape reaching out from the top), and a unique solution is not guaranteed; 7×7 is fixed. Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`masyupearls` adds a Masyu puzzle, bringing the current catalog from 992 to 993 kinds (994 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a solved Masyu on an 8×8 lattice of dots (the corners of 7×7 squares): a closed loop along the lattice lines (again the outline of a randomly grown connected region) with white and black pearls on it. At a white pearl the loop must go straight and at least one of the two neighbouring dots must be a turn; at a black pearl the loop must turn and both arms must go straight through their next dot (so it runs at least one more step each way after turning). All dots that qualify under these rules are collected and the seed takes about 40% of them (at least 5, or all of them if fewer qualify). A white pearl is a light disc with a thin dark ring, a black pearl a dark disc; other dots are small circles. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the tile shows the answer (the loop) together with the pearls, while a real puzzle gives only the pearls and hides the loop; the pearl rules were implemented from memory of the usual Masyu rules (white goes straight with at least one turning neighbour, black turns with both arms straight) and not checked against a rulebook; pearls are only placed at dots that satisfy the rules, so they are consistent with the loop, but a unique solution to the whole puzzle is not guaranteed; the loop comes from a randomly grown region and tends to extend from a particular corner. Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. `stringartcurves` adds string art (modular multiplication chord diagrams), bringing the current catalog from 993 to 994 kinds (995 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is split into 2×2 circles: each circle has 96 evenly spaced points numbered 0 to 95, and point i is joined by a straight line to point (k·i mod 96), where k is the circle's multiplier (2, 3, 4 and 5 in the four circles, shuffled between quadrants by the seed, with each circle turned by a small angle of less than one point spacing). The envelope of these lines is a cardioid for k = 2 and a nephroid for k = 3, with more lobes for larger k. Lines add up and are compressed into brightness (1−e^{−1.6·sum}), so one line is about 0.8 bright and overlaps saturate, with a thin dark ring on the circumference on a deep blue-black background. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the envelope is the visual effect of the chords and no curve is drawn separately; with the same number of points, larger multipliers make the chords very dense (the k = 5 circle looks like a blurred rose); fixed points (k·i ≡ i) draw no line; the number of points is fixed at 96. The sampler measures the distance to up to about 95 chords of the pixel's own circle for every pixel, about 223 ms for one 512×512 build, which is slower than most materials and not optimised. Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile, 0.003 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 512 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`fillominoregions` adds a Fillomino puzzle, bringing the current catalog from 994 to 995 kinds (996 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a solved 9×9 Fillomino board: every cell holds the size of its region (a dot-matrix digit 1 to 9), the cells of one region all show the same number and there are exactly that many of them, regions are separated by thicker dark lines (thin lines inside a region), and larger regions are slightly darker. The seed builds the regions by random growth: in cell order, each unassigned cell gets a random target size 1 to 5 and grows into neighbouring empty cells, and if it ends up the same size as a touching region it keeps adding cells until it differs (so touching regions always differ in size and never merge by accident); if the whole board cannot be completed (about 60% of attempts) it is retried. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the tile shows the solved board, while a real Fillomino gives only some numbers; region sizes are limited to 1 to 9 (they can exceed 5 after the "differ from neighbours" growth) and the size distribution leans larger because touching regions must differ; a unique solution is not guaranteed; the digits are 3×5 dot matrix. Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`futoshikigrid` adds a Futoshiki puzzle, bringing the current catalog from 995 to 996 kinds (997 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a solved 5×5 Futoshiki board: each of the 25 squares holds a dot-matrix digit 1 to 5 and every row and column has 1 to 5 exactly once (a Latin square: the cyclic Latin square with rows, columns and symbols shuffled); between neighbouring squares an inequality sign is drawn with about 55% probability — "<" and ">" for horizontal neighbours, "∧" and "∨" for vertical ones — with the pointed end (the apex) on the side of the smaller number. `nurikabeislands` adds a Nurikabe puzzle, bringing the current catalog from 996 to 997 kinds (998 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a solved 8×8 Nurikabe board: light cells are "islands" and the deep-blue cells are one connected "sea"; each island carries a dot-matrix number on a single cell, equal to the island's cell count; islands never touch orthogonally, the sea is a single connected region and contains no 2×2 block (a "pool"). The seed builds the board: it places 4 to 7 random islands, fills each 2×2 pool by extending a neighbouring island or adding a one-cell island, then requires the sea to stay connected and every island to be at most 9 cells, retrying with different hashes otherwise (a script simulation suggested about 3% of attempts succeed). Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the tile shows the solved board, while a real Nurikabe gives only the island numbers and the solver must deduce the sea; a unique solution is not guaranteed; which cell of an island carries the number (always the cell the island grew from) is seed-driven; 8×8 is fixed and the digits are a 3×5 dot matrix. `tentsandtrees` adds a Tents puzzle, bringing the current catalog from 997 to 998 kinds (999 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a solved 8×8 Tents board: on grass cells there are round-canopy "trees" with a trunk and triangular "tents"; every tent sits orthogonally next to a tree of its own, tents never touch each other even diagonally, and the number of trees equals the number of tents; a column on the right and a row below the board show each row's and column's tent count as dot-matrix digits. The seed builds the board: tents are placed in random order (not next to an existing tent, diagonals included), and each tent picks an empty orthogonal grass cell for its tree, until about 17 tents are placed or no room is left. `shikakurects` adds a Shikaku puzzle, bringing the current catalog from 998 to 999 kinds (1000 gallery choices including plain). The seed decides the cuts: starting from the whole board, a block is split in two at a random position along its longer side; blocks of area 9 or less stop early with 40% probability (area 2 or less always stops) and larger ones always keep splitting; the number goes on a random cell of the rectangle. Metallic and mortar are 0.

`hitorishading` adds a Hitori puzzle, bringing the current catalog from 999 to 1000 kinds (1001 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a solved 7×7 Hitori board: every cell holds a dot-matrix number 1 to 7, and the blacked-out cells have a dark background with a reversed number; blacked-out cells never touch orthogonally, the remaining cells form one connected body, and the cells that are not blacked out have no repeated number in any row or column; the number of every blacked-out cell equals that of some unblacked cell in its row or column (so blacking it out is actually necessary). The seed builds the board: a 7×7 Latin square with rows, columns and symbols shuffled, then cells are blacked out in random order (not next to an already blacked cell, and only if the rest stays connected) up to about 13, and each blacked-out cell's number is replaced by that of an unblacked cell in its row or column. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the tile shows the solved board with the shading drawn, while a real Hitori gives only the numbers and the solver decides which cells to black out; a unique solution is not guaranteed and neither is that this is the only valid shading; the unblacked cells are part of a Latin square, so the board looks more regular than a typical puzzle; the number of blacked-out cells is about 13 (possibly fewer when no more can be added); 7×7 is fixed and the digits are a 3×5 dot matrix. Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Each tile is a solved 8×8 Takuzu board: every cell is either a filled disc (1) or a hollow ring (0) and the board obeys all Takuzu rules — each row and column has exactly four discs and four rings, no row or column has three equal symbols in a line, no two rows are identical and no two columns are identical. The seed builds the board with backtracking: cells are tried in order (which symbol is tried first comes from a hash) and the search steps back on any rule violation until the board is full. `euclideanrhythms` adds Euclidean rhythms, bringing the current catalog from 1007 to 1008 kinds (1009 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a 16-step by 16-track step-sequencer panel: a dark panel carrying 16×16 rounded-square pads, a lit pad meaning a pulse on that step. Every track is a "Euclidean rhythm" — k pulses (k chosen by the seed between 1 and 8) spread as evenly as possible over 16 steps (a Bresenham-style integer spread: step i is lit exactly when (i×k) mod 16 < k), then rotated by a seed-driven offset; so the gap between any two consecutive pulses (wrapping around) is only ever ⌊16/k⌋ or ⌈16/k⌉, with exactly 16 mod k gaps of the larger kind. Unlit pads on every fourth step (columns 1, 5, 9, 13) are slightly lighter, marking the beats. Metallic and mortar are 0.

`colormapregions` adds a map-colouring pattern, bringing the current catalog from 1009 to 1010 kinds (1011 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a seamlessly tiling "map": 6×6 randomly jittered points seed a periodic Voronoi partition (36 regions, with thin darker border lines), and every region gets one brightness such that **no two neighbouring regions (including neighbours that meet across the tile edge, onto the next tile) share a brightness**. The colouring uses backtracking: four brightnesses are tried first and, failing that (node limit 30000), five (0.30, 0.44, 0.58, 0.72, 0.86); over 100 seeds I measured 66 using only four, 34 needing five, and none failing to colour. This is an authored schematic: because the map lives on a torus (left meets right, top meets bottom) it is not covered by the planar four-colour theorem — four colours are not always enough, about a third of the seeds need five (measured above), and the name does not mean only four are used; neighbours are detected by scanning, so a border shorter than about 0.002 of the tile could in principle be missed (rescanning seeds 2 and 3 on a 1024 grid found none missing, but I did not prove this for all seeds); colour is brightness only. Building the sampler costs about 32 ms extra (mean over 100 seeds, measured in Bun, not a performance certification). Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `fouriersquarewaves` adds Fourier square waves, bringing the current catalog from 1019 to 1020 kinds (1021 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is six horizontal panels stacked: panel n draws the partial sum of the first n odd harmonics of the square wave's Fourier series, (4/π)·Σ sin(kt)/k (k = 1, 3, …, 2n−1). Panel 1 is a plain sine (amplitude 4/π); each added harmonic flattens the plateaus further but puts more ripple on them and steepens the transitions, while the overshoot of about 9% of the jump on either side of an edge (the Gibbs phenomenon) does not go away and tends to about 1.179 times the square wave's level. Each panel has a faint axis and two reference rules at the ideal square wave's levels, the waveform is a dark curve (its width is corrected for slope so steep stretches do not thin out), and each tile spans 2 periods horizontally. The content is fixed; the seed only affects faint paper noise. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only 1 to 6 harmonics are drawn, none higher; the curve is computed from the analytic formula per pixel, not plotted from points; the vertical scale is fixed with no axis labels; the "about 9% overshoot" is the theoretical Gibbs value, and the tests only verify that the measured maximum lies between 1.1 and 1.2 rather than equalling it exactly. Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. `pascaltrianglenumbers` adds Pascal triangle numbers, bringing the current catalog from 1020 to 1021 kinds (1022 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is the first 10 rows of Pascal's triangle (rows 0 to 9, the largest entry being 126) in 3×5 dot-matrix digits laid out as a centred triangle; each entry is the sum of the upper-left and upper-right entries of the row above, and odd entries sit on a darker disc while even entries are bare paper, so the odd discs trace out the Sierpinski triangle pattern. The content is fixed and the seed only affects faint paper noise. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only the first 10 rows are drawn; the odd/even discs and the digits are deterministic; no binomial expansion or row sums are labelled; the dot-matrix digits are hard to read at small sizes. `convexhullpoints` adds a convex hull, bringing the current catalog from 1021 to 1022 kinds (1023 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a scatter of points (up to 16, at least 0.12 UV apart and at least 0.07 UV from the tile edge so the tile repeats seamlessly) with their convex hull: hull vertices are marked with larger dark dots, inner points with smaller dots, and the hull polygon is filled light grey with a thin outline. The hull of the seed's point set is computed with Andrew's monotone chain. To keep the hull unambiguous the sampler picks a point set in which no vertex is nearly collinear with its two neighbours and no inner point hugs an edge (up to 48 candidate sets are tried; if none qualifies the last is used). Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: at most 16 points (the minimum spacing means some seeds place fewer); only the hull is shown, not the algorithm's steps; "unambiguous" is a threshold I chose (a vertex at least 0.012 UV from the line through its neighbours, an inner point at least 0.02 UV from any edge), not a mathematical requirement; if all 48 candidates fail the last is used anyway (this caused no test failure across the 600 seeds I tried, but I did not count how often all 48 are used up). Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. `delaunaytriangles` adds a Delaunay triangulation, bringing the current catalog from 1022 to 1023 kinds (1024 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a scatter of points (up to 18, at least 0.1 UV apart and at least 0.06 UV from the tile edge so the tile repeats seamlessly) joined into their Delaunay triangulation: each triangle is filled with a slightly varied light grey, the edges are thin lines and the vertices small dark dots. The triangulation is found by brute force: a triple of points is a Delaunay triangle when no other point lies strictly inside its circumcircle (a few hundred triples times the remaining points, computed once when the sampler is created). Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only the resulting triangulation is drawn, without circumcircles or the algorithm's steps; at most 18 points (the minimum spacing means some seeds place fewer); the positions are seed-driven pseudo-random and near-ties (four nearly cocircular points) are not specially handled, so whether such a triple counts as Delaunay depends on floating-point error and overlapping triangles can in principle appear, which I did not guard against; each pixel scans about 30 triangles and 47 edges, so it costs more per pixel than most materials (about 0.4 s for a single 512×512 render under Bun). Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `collatzsequences` adds Collatz sequences, bringing the current catalog from 1023 to 1024 kinds (1025 gallery choices including plain). Each tile has 10 rows, each the Collatz (hailstone) sequence of a start value: halve an even number, otherwise triple it and add one, until 1 is reached. Every number takes one cell (up to 13 cells), written in 3×5 dot-matrix digits; cells holding odd numbers have a darker background so the "triple and add one" rises are visible, and the rest of the row after the sequence ends is left blank. The seed shuffles the 21 start values from 2 to 60 whose sequences have at most 13 terms and takes 10 of them (all different), for example 3, 13, 21, 53 or 40. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only start values with sequences of at most 13 terms appear (no long trajectories such as 27's), so it says nothing about the Collatz conjecture itself; numbers have at most three digits (53's sequence contains 160); the dot-matrix digits are hard to read at small sizes. Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `hammingcodewords` adds Hamming code words, bringing the current catalog from 1024 to 1025 kinds (1026 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a Hamming(7,4) code word table: the header reads positions 1 to 7 and S (the syndrome), and below it 16 rows hold the 7-bit code word for the data nibbles 0000 to 1111 (row number r) with positions 1 to 7 being p1 p2 d1 p3 d2 d3 d4 (the parity bits at positions 1, 2 and 4 on a slightly darker background). The seed decides for each row whether one bit is flipped (about one row in eight is left alone), and the flipped cell has the darkest background; the rightmost column S is the syndrome (the XOR of the positions holding a 1 in the received word), which equals the flipped position exactly, with 0 meaning no error. So flipping back the bit that S points to gives the original code word, whose data bits are the row number. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only the Hamming(7,4) code, with the 16 rows fixed to data 0 to 15, and at most one flipped bit per row (a Hamming code cannot correct two-bit errors, so none are drawn); the flipped positions are seed-driven pseudo-random; the dot-matrix digits are hard to read at small sizes. Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`cayleytables` adds Cayley tables, bringing the current catalog from 1025 to 1026 kinds (1027 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is the Cayley (multiplication) table of a group of order 8: a 9×9 grid whose top row and left column are dark headers listing the elements 0 to 7, and in the remaining 8×8 body the cell in row a, column b is the product of a and b; cells holding 0 (the identity) have a darker background, tracing the Latin-square pattern of the identity. The seed picks one of the five groups of order 8: the cyclic group Z8, Z4×Z2, Z2×Z2×Z2, the dihedral group D4 and the quaternion group Q8, and shuffles the labels of elements 1 to 7 (0 stays the identity). Every table therefore satisfies the group axioms: an identity, every row and column a permutation, and associativity; the table's shape shows whether the group is commutative and the order of each element. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only those five groups of order 8, with no other orders and no group names shown; the shuffled labels hide any regular pattern; the dot-matrix digits are hard to read at small sizes. Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `romannumerals` adds Roman numerals, bringing the current catalog from 1026 to 1027 kinds (1028 gallery choices including plain). Each tile has 14 rows: on the left a decimal number (1 to 199, right-aligned in three cells), then an equals sign and its Roman numeral (in 3×5 dot-matrix letters I, V, X, L and C, in the standard subtractive form, e.g. 4 as IV, 9 as IX, 40 as XL, 90 as XC; flush left, at most nine letters, e.g. 188 as CLXXXVIII); odd rows have a slightly darker background. The seed picks the 14 numbers from 1 to 199, all different and in ascending order. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only up to 199 (no D or M, so nothing from 500 up); only the standard subtractive notation, not the ancient variants such as IIII; the dot-matrix letters are hard to read at small sizes (I and the digit 1 have different shapes but can still be confused when tiny). `signedencodings` adds signed integer encodings, bringing the current catalog from 1027 to 1028 kinds (1029 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a 4-bit lookup table: 16 rows list 0000 to 1111, and each row has the binary bits (the column of the most significant bit, the sign bit, has the darkest background), the unsigned value (0 to 15, header U) and the signed value (header: the encoding's code). The seed picks one of three signed encodings: two's complement (2C, where 1000 is −8 up to 1111 as −1), one's complement (1C, where 1000 is −7 and 1111 is "−0") and sign and magnitude (SM, where 1000 is "−0" and 1001 is −1 up to 1111 as −7); negative rows (including "−0") have a slightly darker background and a "−" sign written before the signed value. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only 4 bits and only those three encodings, with no overflow or arithmetic shown; one's complement and sign-magnitude have a negative zero while two's complement does not, which is the point of putting them side by side; the dot-matrix digits are hard to read at small sizes. Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `kochsnowflake` adds a Koch snowflake, bringing the current catalog from 1029 to 1030 kinds (1031 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is divided into four 2×2 panels showing the Koch snowflake after 0, 1, 2 and 3 iterations: 0 is an equilateral triangle, and each iteration replaces the middle third of every edge with an outward equilateral bump. The panels' order and each one's rotation are drawn by the seed, and each polygon (up to 192 segments) is filled by the even-odd rule and outlined with a thin dark line. The boundary length therefore grows by 4/3 per iteration and the area follows A₀·(8/5 − (3/5)(4/9)ⁿ) (A₀ at 0, tending to 1.6·A₀). Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only 0 to 3 iterations are drawn, none higher, and it is not the true fractal limit; the side length of 0.36 UV (circumradius about 0.208 UV) is fixed and the panels do not overlap; each pixel scans up to 192 edges, about 0.3 s for one 512×512 render under Bun (from the preview script, measured once). Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `newtonbasins` adds Newton basins, bringing the current catalog from 1030 to 1031 kinds (1032 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is the basin-of-attraction picture of Newton's method for z^n − 1 (the n-th roots of unity): a square window of the complex plane from −1.6 to 1.6 in both real and imaginary parts, where each point is painted with the brightness of the n-th root that the Newton iteration z ← z − (z^n − 1)/(n z^(n−1)) finally converges to (more roots mean more brightness levels), with slowly converging points slightly darker (by up to 10 steps). The seed picks n from 3, 4 and 5; the coordinates pass through a triangle-wave fold, so the pattern is continuous across the tile edge. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only the polynomials z^n − 1 with n from 3 to 5; brightness only tells which root and how fast, not hue (procedural materials only have a dark-to-light ramp); basin boundaries are fractal, so pixels near them are sensitive to floating-point error, each pixel iterates at most 40 times and a point that does not converge (near a boundary or a pole) is assigned by its final position; the triangle-wave fold mirrors the pattern left-right and top-bottom. Defaults are a 0.6 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. `mandelbrotbands` adds Mandelbrot bands, bringing the current catalog from 1031 to 1032 kinds (1033 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a smooth escape-time contour picture of the Mandelbrot set: the seed picks one of four fixed windows — the whole set (centre −0.6, half-width 1.6, 80 iterations), the seahorse valley (−0.745 + 0.113i, half-width 0.06), a branch near the imaginary axis (−0.16 + 1.0405i, half-width 0.04) and the neighbourhood of the Feigenbaum point (−1.401155, half-width 0.02), the last three zoomed windows with 160 iterations each. The inside of the set (points that do not escape within the iteration limit) is dark; outside, each point's brightness comes from the smooth escape time ν = n + 1 − log₂(log|z| / log 256) (larger ν is brighter, with a cosine contour band of period 3 added), so rings of bands surround the set. The coordinates pass through a triangle-wave fold so the pattern is continuous across the tile edge. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only those four windows, with no interactive zoom; the inside is decided by the iteration limit, so pixels on the set's edge can differ slightly with the limit (in a temporary test over 120 extra seeds the best window's agreement was 1.0000 (the runner-up at most 0.265), at a 0.02 tolerance on an 80×80 grid, which does not mean every pixel agrees); brightness only encodes escape speed, not hue; the triangle-wave fold mirrors the pattern. Each pixel iterates at most 160 times, about 0.15 s for one 512×512 render under Bun (from the preview script, measured once). Defaults are a 0.6 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. `cantorsetrows` adds Cantor set rows, bringing the current catalog from 1032 to 1033 kinds (1034 gallery choices including plain). Each tile stacks 8 horizontal bands from top to bottom, the k-th (k = 0 to 7) being the set after k steps of the Cantor construction: band 0 is the whole strip and each further step removes the middle part of every interval. The seed picks one of three fractions removed: a third (the classic Cantor set, where band k has 2^k intervals of length (1/3)^k), a fifth (two fifths kept each step, leaving more) and a half (a quarter kept each step, leaving less); band k has 2^k equal intervals with total length (1 − r)^k, r being the fraction removed. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only 8 steps (at step 7 the intervals are narrower than a pixel and only faint stripes show) and only those three removal fractions; each band's edge is softened by distance to the interval boundary; the paper shows between bands. Defaults are a 0.8 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. `conicsections` adds conic sections, bringing the current catalog from 1033 to 1034 kinds (1035 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is divided into four 2×2 panels showing a circle, an ellipse, a parabola and a hyperbola with eccentricity e of 0, 0.6, 1 and 1.6, the arrangement of the panels being chosen by the seed. The curves are drawn from the definition "distance to the focus r = e × distance to the directrix" (the semi-latus rectum l is fixed at 0.09 UV; written r = |l − e·x'|, where x' is the offset from the focus along the axis); the focus is a small dot and the directrix (for e > 0) a dashed line; the parabola and hyperbola run to the panel edge and both branches of the hyperbola are drawn. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only those four curves, with the axis fixed horizontal (no rotation) and no axes or labels; the line width is softened by a first-order distance estimate of the implicit function, so it can vary slightly on steep stretches far from the vertex; each panel's focus position is set by hand to centre the curve (the hyperbola's focus sits left of centre and the ellipse's right). Defaults are a 0.6 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. `rosecurves` adds rose curves, bringing the current catalog from 1034 to 1035 kinds (1036 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is nine 3×3 panels, each drawing a rhodonea rose r = R·cos(kθ) with k equal to 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 3/2, 5/2, 5/3 and 7/3 (an integer k gives k or 2k petals, a fractional k gives overlapping multi-petal roses, and k = 1 is a circle); the seed decides how the nine curves are arranged in the panels. Lines are drawn using a first-order distance estimate to the polar implicit function, and the origin is marked. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only those nine values of k, a fixed amplitude and no rotation phase; no formula or labels are shown; a fractional-k curve needs several turns to close (the denominator times 2π), and the sampler evaluates the distance estimate over twice the denominator half-turns for each pixel, so the line width can vary slightly where petals cross. Defaults are a 0.6 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `cassiniovals` adds Cassini ovals, bringing the current catalog from 1035 to 1036 kinds (1037 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is centred on two foci and draws a family of Cassini ovals: on each curve the product of the distances to the two foci, |PF₁|·|PF₂| = b², is constant, with b = ratio × a (a is half the distance between the foci, picked by the seed from 0.13, 0.18 and 0.23 UV) and the ratios 0.4, 0.7, 0.9, 1, 1.15, 1.35 and 1.6. For a ratio below 1 the curve splits into two ovals each enclosing one focus; for a ratio of 1 it is the lemniscate of Bernoulli (a figure eight, drawn thicker); above 1 it is a single curve enclosing both foci. The two foci are marked with small dots. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only those 7 ratios, always horizontal, with no axes or labels; the line width is softened by a first-order distance estimate of the implicit function (at the midpoint between the foci the gradient is zero, so I floor it at 1e-6 to avoid dividing by zero, see the log below); only three focal separations to choose from. Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `twosourceripples` adds two-source ripples, bringing the current catalog from 1036 to 1037 kinds (1038 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is the interference pattern of two identical circular wave sources: the sources sit horizontally in the middle of the tile 0.22 or 0.32 UV apart, with a wavelength of 0.04, 0.052 or 0.07 UV (both picked by the seed), and each point's brightness comes from the sum of the two waves, cos(k·r₁) + cos(k·r₂) = 2 cos(k(r₁+r₂)/2) cos(k(r₁−r₂)/2) (r₁ and r₂ being the distances to the two sources), so on the hyperbolas where r₁ − r₂ is an odd multiple of half a wavelength the waves cancel and the brightness sits at its middle value (the nodal lines), while the crests and troughs are brightest or darkest where the waves are in step. The coordinates pass through a triangle-wave fold so the pattern is continuous across the tile edge. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only two point sources of equal amplitude and phase, with no attenuation or reflecting boundary (the triangle-wave fold is only for a continuous seam, not physical mirroring); brightness is just interference intensity, not hue. Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.006 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0.
