`luhnnumbers` adds Luhn numbers, bringing the current catalog from 1037 to 1038 kinds (1039 gallery choices including plain). Each tile has 10 rows of 16-digit numbers (in groups of four with a gap between groups); the last digit of each row is the check digit (on a darker background) and each row ends with a mark: a check mark means the whole number passes the Luhn test (from the right, double every second digit, subtract 9 from any result above 9, and the total is a multiple of 10) and a cross means it does not. The first 15 digits of each row are drawn by the seed and the check digit is computed from them; about 60% of the rows are left valid and in the others one digit is changed to a different one (changing any single digit always breaks the Luhn sum), so the marks agree with the actual check result. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the digits are random, not real card numbers (no issuer prefix or length rules are modelled), only an illustration of the Luhn algorithm; the share of valid rows in a tile comes from the seed's pseudo-randomness (about 60%, not a fixed count); odd rows (second, fourth, …) have a slightly darker background; the dot-matrix digits are hard to read at small sizes. Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. `bezierconstruction` adds a Bezier construction, bringing the current catalog from 1038 to 1039 kinds (1040 gallery choices including plain). The seed picks t from 1/4, 1/3, 1/2 and 2/3, shared by all four panels. Metallic and mortar are 0.

`vennregions` adds Venn regions, bringing the current catalog from 1039 to 1040 kinds (1041 gallery choices including plain). Metallic and mortar are 0.

`ieee754floats` adds IEEE 754 single-precision floats, bringing the current catalog from 1040 to 1041 kinds (1042 gallery choices including plain). Each tile has six single-precision numbers from top to bottom: above each, a line with its decimal value (to 4 decimal places, in 3×5 dot-matrix digits with a decimal point and a minus sign), and below it its 32 bits: 1 sign bit (on the darkest background), 8 exponent bits (bias 127, on the next darkest) and 23 mantissa bits (on the lightest), with thin lines between the fields. The value is (−1)^sign × 2^(exponent−127) × (1 + mantissa/2²³); the seed draws each number's sign, exponent (124 to 133, so magnitudes roughly between 0.125 and 128) and mantissa, so the printed decimal and the bits correspond. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only normal single-precision numbers, with the exponent fixed to 124 to 133 and no zero, infinity, NaN or subnormals; the decimal value is printed to only 4 decimal places, the exact value rounded; the bits are drawn as 3×5 dot-matrix 0s and 1s and are hard to read at small sizes. `bellcurvebands` adds bell-curve bands, bringing the current catalog from 1041 to 1042 kinds (1043 gallery choices including plain). Each tile draws the bell curve of a normal distribution (the Gaussian e^(−z²/2) with z = (x − mean)/σ), with the area under the curve split into four bands by how many standard deviations from the mean: within 1σ the darkest, 1 to 2σ the next, 2 to 3σ lighter and beyond 3σ the lightest; an axis runs along the bottom with a tick at each σ from −3σ to +3σ. The width σ is picked by the seed from 0.07, 0.09 and 0.11 UV, and the height of the curve is fixed. Because the area is proportional to the integral of e^(−z²/2), the ratio of the band areas is the normal distribution's 68–95–99.7 rule (about 68.27%, 95.45% and 99.73%). Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: just one standard normal curve with σ chosen from only three values and no axis labels or numbers; the line width is corrected for slope; the bands use brightness only (procedural materials only have a dark-to-light ramp); the height is fixed, so curves with different σ enclose different areas (they are only similar in shape), which makes this an illustration of proportions rather than of absolute probability density. Defaults are a 0.6 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`roundingmodes` adds rounding modes, bringing the current catalog from 1042 to 1043 kinds (1044 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is a rounding comparison table: a dark header row reads X and the codes of five ways of rounding — FL (floor), CE (ceiling), TR (truncation toward zero), RN (round to nearest, halves away from zero) and RE (round to nearest, halves to even, "banker's rounding") — and 12 rows below each hold a number x (to one decimal place) with its integer result under each of the five. The seed picks the 12 values from a fixed pool of 20 (from −3.5 to 6.5, including negatives, 0 and several exact halves) and lists them in ascending order; in rows where x is exactly a half the RN and RE columns have a darker background, since those are the only cases where the two can differ (for example 2.5: RN gives 3 and RE gives 2; 3.5: both give 4). A result of zero is always printed as "0", never with a minus sign. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only those five modes, and x with one decimal place; the pool of values is fixed, not arbitrary numbers; the dot-matrix text is hard to read at small sizes (the four characters of the x column exactly fill the cell width). `binaryaddition` adds binary addition, bringing the current catalog from 1043 to 1044 kinds (1045 gallery choices including plain). Each tile stacks three column additions from top to bottom, each adding two random 8-bit binary numbers: a row of small digits on top holds the carries (into positions 1 to 8), followed by addend A, addend B with a "+" sign, a rule, and at the bottom the 9-bit sum (one bit longer than the addends to hold the final carry), with a darker background on the sum row. Each small carry digit sits right above the column that receives it; the units column receives no carry, so it has none. Every column obeys the full-adder rule: A bit + B bit + carry in = sum bit + 2 × carry out. A and B in the three problems come from the seed (hash randomness); carry chains are not deliberately selected. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only 8-bit unsigned addition, with no negative numbers, overflow flag or decimal equivalent; carries are only smaller, lighter digits without a colour of their own (procedural materials only have a dark-to-light ramp). Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `abeliansandpile` adds an abelian sandpile, bringing the current catalog from 1044 to 1045 kinds (1046 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is the stable pile left after thousands of grains are dropped on the centre cell of an 81 × 81 grid: whenever a cell holds four or more grains it gives one grain to each of its four neighbours per four it holds, until every cell holds at most three; grains that leave the grid vanish. Each cell is painted in one of four brightnesses (darkest to lightest) for 0 to 3 grains. The seed picks the grain count from 4000, 5200 and 6400. The final pile of such a sandpile does not depend on the order of the topplings (the abelian property), so the result is deterministic and has the eightfold symmetry of the square. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only a single source at the centre and only three grain counts, with no other initial configurations; there are no lines between cells, and the edges show slight stair-steps when the grid does not line up with pixels (81 cells do not map to a whole number of pixels). The pile covers only part of the tile; the rest is the 0-grain background. The sampler has to simulate the whole pile when it is first called and is a lookup afterwards; the preview script measured about 224 ms per run at 512² (Bun, not a formal benchmark). Defaults are a 0.6 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. The seed picks p from 0.56, 0.5927 and 0.63 (0.5927 is the site-percolation threshold of the square lattice). Metallic and mortar are 0.

`logisticbifurcation` adds a logistic bifurcation diagram, bringing the current catalog from 1048 to 1049 kinds (1050 gallery choices including plain). Each tile is the bifurcation diagram of the logistic map x → r·x·(1−x): the horizontal axis is the growth rate r and the vertical axis the long-run values of x (after dropping the first 300 steps as transient, 500 steps are recorded; 0 at the bottom, 1 at the top); the 256 × 256 pixel cells are shaded by the number of recorded values that land in them (one is already visible, more is darker, saturating at about 15). The seed picks the range of r from 2.5 to 4, 3.4 to 4 and 3.55 to 3.95. The fixed point, period doubling, the chaotic band and the period-3 window can be seen. The starting value is fixed at 0.4. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only the logistic map, with no axis labels, numbers or other maps; each column uses only the r at its centre, not an average over its range; points in the chaotic region depend on floating-point details, so only the outline and the periodic regions are stable. `burningship` adds the Burning Ship fractal, bringing the current catalog from 1049 to 1050 kinds (1051 gallery choices including plain). Each tile shows smooth escape-time contours of the Burning Ship fractal: for each point c it iterates z → (|Re z| + i|Im z|)² + c (the Mandelbrot iteration with the absolute value of the real and imaginary parts taken first), stops once past the bound (256), and sets brightness from the smooth escape time (the step count with a fractional correction for how far past the bound it jumped) with a contour band that varies with escape time added; points that do not escape get the darkest background. The seed picks the view from four preset regions (one whole-set view and three zoomed views; coordinates are in the preset, and I did not check the zoomed regions against a catalogue of known features); coordinates are folded so the picture is continuous across the tile edge and mirrored left-right and top-bottom. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only the Burning Ship fractal, with no axis labels; because the coordinates are mirrored, the picture is not in the standard "ship" orientation and the whole-set view looks like mirrored wings; only four fixed views, and the detail regions (such as the small ship) rely on a fixed iteration limit, so deeper zooms are out of scope; pixels near the escape edge are sensitive to floating-point error. `fordcircles` adds Ford circles, bringing the current catalog from 1056 to 1057 kinds (1058 gallery choices including plain). Each tile draws the Ford circles: for every fraction p/q in lowest terms (0 ≤ p/q ≤ 1, with denominator q up to a limit) a circle of diameter 1/q² is drawn tangent to the number line at p/q, and the circles of any two Farey neighbours (|p·q′ − p′·q| = 1) touch each other. The number line is the bottom edge of the tile; circles are filled with a brightness by denominator q (the largest, with denominator 1, the darkest, the others lighter) and given a thin dark outline. The seed picks the denominator limit from 4, 6 and 8. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only fractions from 0 to 1 and only three limits, with no fraction labels; the two big circles of denominator 1 (0/1 and 1/1) have radius 0.5, so they fill the tile height and sit on the left and right edges; the difference between limits 8 and 6, or 6 and 4, is only a few very small circles, hardly visible at small sizes. `mobiusgrid` adds a Moebius grid, bringing the current catalog from 1057 to 1058 kinds (1059 gallery choices including plain). Each tile shows a checkered square grid after a Moebius transformation w = (az + b)/(cz + d): vertical and horizontal grid lines in the z plane (spacing 0.5) and the checkerboard shading of its squares, whose lines become circles or straight lines after the map (circles still cross at right angles, since the map is conformal) with the shading carried along. For every pixel the sampler first inverts the map, z = (dw − b)/(−cw + a), then converts the distance to the nearest grid line in the z plane to a distance in the w plane (on screen) with the local scale |ad − bc|/|cz + d|², so the line width is uniform on screen. The seed picks the map from three presets: the inversion w = 1/z, an elliptic map and a loxodromic (spiral) map; coordinates are folded so the picture is continuous across the tile edge and mirrored left-right and top-bottom. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only three preset maps, with no marking of poles or fixed points; near the point that corresponds to infinity in the z plane the grid lines are infinitely dense and become a dark blob (the dark mass at the centres in the picture); the line width is uniform only on screen and does not represent the line width in the z plane; the picture is mirrored because the coordinates are folded. The line width is converted with the gradient length 2h/(r₁r₂) and is uniform on screen. Coordinates are folded so the picture is continuous across the tile edge and mirrored. Metallic and mortar are 0.

`boxplots` adds box plots, bringing the current catalog from 1061 to 1062 kinds (1063 gallery choices including plain). Each tile stacks three box plots from top to bottom: every group has 15 data values drawn as small dots on two alternating rows (alternate values in sorted order go on alternate rows so that neighbouring dots do not overlap), and above the dots sits the box plot of the group — a box from the first quartile (Q1) to the third quartile (Q3), a line in it for the median, and a thin line (whisker) at each side out to the minimum and the maximum with a short cap at its end. Quartiles use Tukey's hinges: the 8th of the 15 values is the median, Q1 is the median of the 7 values below it (the 4th) and Q3 is the median of the 7 values above it (the 12th), with no interpolation. The three groups have different distribution shapes (exponents 0.7, 1 and 1.3 lean the values to one side). Metallic and mortar are 0.

The whole tile draws the layout of the first four periods of the periodic table (elements 1 to 36): 18 columns and 4 rows with one cell per element, the atomic number above (small dot-matrix characters) and the element symbol below (capital letters, for example HE, FE, CU), and the places where the table has no element left blank. Each cell has one of three background shades, and the seed decides what the three shades mean: (0) the block, by column (groups 1–2, groups 3–12 and groups 13–18), (1) metal, metalloid and nonmetal, or (2) solid, liquid (bromine) or gas at 25 °C. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only the first four periods are drawn (no lanthanides or actinides and nothing beyond period 4); the symbols are all in capitals to keep the glyphs simple (He is written HE) and at small sizes texts like "MN" and "NA" can be hard to tell apart; the classification is the common textbook one (metalloids B, Si, Ge and As; nonmetals include the noble gases; hydrogen counts as a nonmetal and a gas), and textbooks differ for some individual elements; there is no legend. The data was typed from memory by the author and a second copy written by hand in the test file for comparison, and was not checked against an external source. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Prefer 1024 or larger; 32 is a coarse preview. This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`circleoffifths` adds a circle of fifths, bringing the current catalog from 1088 to 1089 kinds (1090 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile is a circle of fifths: the outer ring writes the 12 major keys in order (clockwise; each is a perfect fifth above the previous one: C, G, D, A, E, B, F#, Db, Ab, Eb, Bb, F), the middle ring their relative minors (Am, Em, Bm, F#m, C#m, G#m, Ebm, Bbm, Fm, Cm, Gm, Dm) and the inner ring the number of sharps or flats of the key signature (0, 1# to 6#, 5b to 1b), with 12 sectors on alternating faint backgrounds and thin rings between the three zones. The seed decides which key is at the top (12 choices) and whether the fifths run clockwise or anticlockwise (anticlockwise gives a circle of fourths). Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only the major keys, relative minors and signature counts are written, with no clef or notes; the F#/Gb position is written only as F# (6 sharps); note names use capital letters plus "#" and "b" (the accidentals are simplified dot-matrix symbols, with "#" drawn as a double-bar double-stroke mark) and a lower-case m, and at small sizes "b" and "B", or "#" and other characters, can be hard to tell apart. The key-signature and relative-minor data were typed from memory and the test file checks them separately by pitch arithmetic (a fifth is 7 semitones, a relative minor is 3 semitones lower, the number of sharps is (pitch × 7) mod 12), but they were not checked against an external source and the choice of enharmonic spellings (for example C#m against Dbm) was not checked against convention. Defaults are a 0.9 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. The whole tile is the ring of 37 pockets of a European roulette wheel: the pockets are arranged in the actual wheel order (0, 32, 15, 19, 4, 21, 2, 25, 17, 34, 6, 27, 13, 36, 11, 30, 8, 23, 10, 5, 24, 16, 33, 1, 20, 14, 31, 9, 22, 18, 29, 7, 28, 12, 35, 3, 26, and round to 0 again), each showing its number in dot-matrix characters (kept upright rather than rotating with the angle); red pockets are mid grey, black pockets dark and the zero light, with light digits on the red and black pockets and dark digits on the zero, and thin dividers between pockets; a grey disc sits in the middle. `roundrobintable` adds a round-robin schedule, bringing the current catalog from 1090 to 1091 kinds (1092 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile is a league schedule: n teams (the seed picks n as 8 or 10) are scheduled by the circle method into n − 1 rounds of n/2 matches each — the first team stays and the others move one place round the circle every round — and each row writes the round number (on a darker label) followed by the matches of that round as "A-B", so every team plays exactly once in every round and every pair of teams meets exactly once in the whole schedule. The team numbering is shuffled by the seed (Fisher–Yates); odd rows have a faint background band. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only the schedule, with no team names, venues or scores; n is only 8 or 10 (no odd number of teams with byes); home and away are not distinguished; the characters are 3 × 5 dot-matrix glyphs and their size depends on n (smaller for n = 10). `kaprekarsteps` adds Kaprekar steps, bringing the current catalog from 1091 to 1092 kinds (1093 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile is split into 2 columns × 2 blocks, each block being a chain of Kaprekar's routine: start from a four-digit number (not one with four equal digits, and not 6174), arrange its digits from large to small to make one number and from small to large to make another, subtract to get the difference, and repeat with that difference (padded with zeros to four digits) until 6174 is reached; each step is written as a line "large-small=difference" (for example 7641-1467=6174), the four characters of the difference sit on a darker cell and odd lines have a faint background band. The four starting numbers come from the seed. A chain has at most 7 steps (the longest for four-digit numbers). Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only four-digit numbers and only the arithmetic of each step are written (the starting number itself is implied by the digits of the first line and is not written separately); there are no step counts or note that 6174 is a fixed point; shorter chains leave the lower part of the block empty. Defaults are a 0.8 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `lookandsayrows` adds look-and-say rows, bringing the current catalog from 1092 to 1093 kinds (1094 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile lists the terms of the look-and-say sequence from top to bottom: each term reads the previous one aloud — it counts the run of equal digits and then writes the digit, for example 1 → 11 (one 1) → 21 (two 1s) → 1211 → 111221 → 312211 …; the first digit of each row sits on a darker cell and odd rows have a faint band. The first term is picked by the seed from 1 to 6; the terms grow quickly, so rows are listed only until the next term would have more than 26 digits (at most 11 rows). Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only the terms are listed, with no term numbers or statement of the rule; the terms use only the digits 0 to 9; the limit of 26 digits is set by the width of the layout and is not a property of the sequence, so different starting digits can give different numbers of rows (the preview with start 6 shows 9 rows). `happynumberchains` adds happy-number chains, bringing the current catalog from 1093 to 1094 kinds (1095 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile writes 12 chains of "sum of the squares of the digits" from top to bottom: starting from a number between 2 and 99 that the seed picks, each step takes the sum of the squares of the digits to get the next number, joined with ">", for example 19>82>68>100>1; a chain stops at 1 (the start is a happy number) or at the first 4 (every other number ends up in the cycle 4, 16, 37, 58, 89, 145, 42, 20, so the chain stops at 4). The 12 starting numbers are all different, and a start is only used when its chain is at most 34 characters wide (a start whose chain is too long is replaced by the next number drawn from the seed); odd rows have a faint band. `recamanarcs` adds Recaman arcs, bringing the current catalog from 1094 to 1095 kinds (1096 gallery choices including plain). `digitalroottable` adds a digital-root table, bringing the current catalog from 1096 to 1097 kinds (1098 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile is a square table whose row i and column j count from 1 and whose cells hold the digital root (add the digits again and again until one digit is left, giving 1 to 9): the seed picks one of three tables — i × j, i + j or i² + j² — and the number of cells per side (9, 12 or 18). Each cell is toned by its root (1 darkest, 9 lightest, a linear ramp) and shows the root as a 3 × 5 dot-matrix digit with an opposite-toned ink; a lower mid-grey groove runs between cells. The i² + j² table only contains some roots (squares modulo 9 are only 0, 1, 4, 7), so its tone ramp has gaps. `henonattractor` adds the Henon attractor, bringing the current catalog from 1097 to 1098 kinds (1099 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile is a density plot of the Henon map x′ = 1 − a·x² + y, y′ = b·x iterated 600,000 times: the points are counted in a 256 × 256 grid, put through a logarithm and bilinearly interpolated into ink density, so the dark-blue curves on light paper are the fine layers of the attractor. The seed picks one of four chaotic parameter pairs (a, b) = (1.4, 0.3), (1.35, 0.3), (1.4, 0.25), (1.2, 0.3) and whether the picture is mirrored sideways and/or upside down; the window is fixed to x in [−1.35, 1.35] and y in [−0.45, 0.45], so y is stretched about 1.5 times relative to x; the window has a 3% blank margin, so the tile repeats seamlessly. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: there are no axes, ticks or parameter labels; y is stretched rather than to scale; the curves are thin, only one or two pixels wide at 512 or smaller. The four parameter pairs were chosen from combinations I tried with a script as ones that fill many grid cells (chaotic); this is not a mathematical proof. I also tried a = 1.3, b = 0.3 and a = 1.25, b = 0.3, but they occupy only 7 cells (periodic orbits), so they are not used. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. Every sampler creation iterates 600,000 times (about 111 to 160 ms for a 512 preview in one run, not a performance certification). This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`golombrulers` adds Golomb rulers, bringing the current catalog from 1098 to 1099 kinds (1100 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile draws nine rulers from top to bottom with 3 to 11 marks, all at one scale, so they get longer toward the bottom (the longest is 72 units): a Golomb ruler has no two pairs of marks at the same distance, and these are the shortest (optimal) rulers as I remember them — mark positions 0 1 3, 0 1 4 6, 0 1 4 9 11, 0 1 4 10 12 17, 0 1 4 10 18 23 25, 0 1 4 9 15 22 32 34, 0 1 5 12 25 27 35 41 44, 0 1 6 10 23 26 34 41 53 55, 0 1 4 13 28 33 47 54 64 70 72. Each ruler has a pale body, a small tick at every unit and a tall dark line at each mark; the seed decides at random for each ruler whether it is mirrored (a mirrored Golomb ruler is still one). Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: there are no numbers and no distances are labelled; the longest ruler is 72 units, so the short ones (3 and 4 marks) fill only a small part on the left; the positions come from the published optimal rulers as I remember them, with no external source to check against, so the documents and tests only guarantee "no repeated distance", and that the lengths for 3 to 8 marks are shortest by exhaustive search — the lengths for 9 to 11 marks (44, 55, 72) are not proven shortest by the tests. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. `bitwisetable` adds a bitwise table, bringing the current catalog from 1099 to 1100 kinds (1101 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile is a square table whose row i and column j count from 0 to the side length minus 1 and whose cells hold i AND j, i OR j or i XOR j: the seed picks one of the three operations and the number of cells per side (8, 16 or 32). Each cell is toned linearly by its value (0 darkest, side length minus 1 lightest) and writes the value in binary as small squares (most significant bit on the left, a square is a 1, with 3, 4 or 5 bits), with an ink opposite to the background tone; a lower mid-grey groove runs between cells. On a large scale the three tables show different fractal layouts (AND is darker, OR lighter, XOR is symmetric with a diagonal of 0). Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: there are no headers and no operator symbol; the squares are tiny — at 32 cells each bit is only one or two pixels in a 512 texture, so 1024 or larger is advisable; only 1 bits are marked, 0 bits are left blank. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.005 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. `peanocurve` adds the Peano curve, bringing the current catalog from 1100 to 1101 kinds (1102 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile draws the Peano space-filling curve through the cell centres: the seed picks the order 2, 3 or 4 (9, 27 or 81 cells per side, so 81, 729 or 6561 cells), the curve starts in the darkest tone and gradually turns to a lighter blue-grey up to its end; it is made of 3 × 3 copies of the previous order in three columns of three in a serpentine order, each mirrored up/down or left/right so that it starts where the previous one ended; the seed also picks one of the eight mirrorings and turns (including a transpose). The line is about half a cell wide and a 4% margin is left around, so the tile repeats seamlessly. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the curve has no start, end or numbering marks, so its direction can only be told from the tone gradient; with 81 cells each cell is only about six pixels wide at 512, so 1024 or larger is advisable. The curve is built by recursion and the tests compare it with another formula that complements ternary digits. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. `cliffordattractor` adds the Clifford attractor, bringing the current catalog from 1101 to 1102 kinds (1103 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile is a density plot of the Clifford map x′ = sin(a·y) + c·cos(a·x), y′ = sin(b·x) + d·cos(b·y) iterated 800,000 times: the points are counted in a 256 × 256 grid, put through a logarithm and bilinearly interpolated into ink density (dark blue ink on light paper). The seed picks one of five parameter sets (a, b, c, d) = (−1.4, 1.6, 1, 0.7), (1.7, 1.7, 0.6, 1.2), (−1.7, 1.3, −0.1, −1.2), (−1.7, 1.8, −1.9, −0.4), (1.6, −0.6, −1.2, 1.6) and whether the picture is mirrored sideways and/or upside down; the window is the exact range of the map (x within 1 + |c|, y within 1 + |d|) with a 3% blank margin, so the tile repeats seamlessly. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: there are no axes or parameter labels; the five parameter sets were chosen after trying eight (three of them are not used): one occupied only 76 cells (a periodic orbit) and two covered about 80% of the cells (too full to read) in the small 48 × 48 count I used; "chaotic" here is only that cell count, not a mathematical proof; every sampler creation iterates 800,000 times (about 135 to 149 ms for a 512 preview in single runs, not a performance certification). Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `voronoicells` adds Voronoi cells, bringing the current catalog from 1102 to 1103 kinds (1104 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile is a Voronoi partition: every cell of a grid has one jittered site (grid size 5, 7 or 9 per side, jitter 0.25, 0.32 or 0.38 of a cell width, each picked by the seed; the grid wraps around the tile, so it joins seamlessly left/right and up/down), every point takes the tone of its nearest site (each site has a random mid-to-light grey), a thin darker border runs where the two nearest sites are about equally far, and a small dark dot sits at the middle of every site. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: there are no numbers or labels and the tones are only random greys; the border width uses half the difference between the nearest and second-nearest distance as an approximation of the distance to the border, so the border is slightly wider at sharp corners where three cells meet; every pixel checks the sites of the surrounding 5 × 5 grid cells (a 3 × 3 search also passed an earlier version of these tests, but I have not proved that 3 × 3 is always enough at jitter 0.38). Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.005 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`euclidsquares` adds Euclid squares, bringing the current catalog from 1103 to 1104 kinds (1105 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile draws the Euclidean algorithm as a square dissection: a W × H rectangle is first cut, from its top left corner along the longer side, into as many squares as fit with the side of the shorter side, then the leftover rectangle is cut in the same way, until nothing is left (the last squares have side gcd(W, H)). The seed picks one of six rectangles (57 × 22, 43 × 16, 49 × 19, 58 × 35, 60 × 24, 55 × 21) and whether it is transposed, mirrored left/right and mirrored up/down (eight orientations); the squares are toned from dark (the first one cut) to light (the last), each has a thin dark border and so does the outline, and the rectangle is centred with its long side at 94% of the tile. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: there are no numbers, quotients or gcd labels; rectangles such as 60 × 24 and 55 × 21 give many squares of the same size and only the tone order tells the order of cutting; the rectangle is centred with blank space around it, so the texture is not a continuous pattern across the tile edge, only a repeated arrangement. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.005 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`youngtableaux` adds Young tableaux, bringing the current catalog from 1104 to 1105 kinds (1106 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile is 2 × 2 panels, each drawing a standard Young tableau of 10 boxes: the shape is a partition of 10 (at most 5 parts, each at most 5), filled with the numbers 1 to 10 once each, strictly increasing along every row and down every column. The seed picks four different shapes among all that qualify (by a shuffle) and fills each by putting the numbers 1 to 10 one at a time into a random addable box (the boxes above and to the left are already filled), so every panel is a valid standard Young tableau (not a uniform draw from all standard tableaux); the seed also chooses English (row one on top) or French (row one at the bottom) drawing and whether everything is transposed (a transposed tableau is still a standard Young tableau). Boxes are toned by number from dark (1) to light (10), the numbers are 3 × 5 dot-matrix digits (two digits for 10), and thin dark lines run between boxes. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the partition of the shape and the hook lengths are not labelled; a picture cannot tell whether it was transposed (a transposed tableau is still standard); the diagrams are at most 5 boxes wide and the dot-matrix digits are small, so they are read from pixel edges at 512 and 1024 or larger is advisable. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.005 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`braiddiagram` adds a braid diagram, bringing the current catalog from 1105 to 1106 kinds (1107 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile draws a mathematical braid diagram: 4, 5 or 6 strands (picked by the seed) run from top to bottom, and at each of 3 × strands levels two neighbouring strands cross, one over the other (the under strand is hidden by the dark outline of the over one); the same pair of places is never crossed twice in a row, and left-over or right-over is random; every strand keeps a grey tone fixed by its starting place (darkest at the left, lightest at the right), so the order of tones along the bottom is the permutation the braid makes. Crossings use S-curves, and the strand width is measured across the curve, so slanted parts do not get thinner. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: it does not label the braid word (σ₁, σ₂ …) or the permutation; each level has exactly one crossing, so two crossings never happen at one level; strands differ only in brightness, not hue (the material has a single dark-to-light ramp); the outline makes the under strand look cut at a crossing, but that is a drawing convention, not a three-dimensional knot. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.005 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. `countingrods` adds counting rods, bringing the current catalog from 1106 to 1107 kinds (1108 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile is eight rows, each writing a decimal number (2 to 5 digits, picked by the seed) at the left in 3 × 5 dot-matrix digits and again at the right in Chinese counting rod numerals: one square place per digit with the units place at the right; 1 to 5 are that many rods, 6 to 9 are a bar (five) with 1 to 4 rods under it, and 0 is an empty place; places alternate — the units, hundreds and ten-thousands use the vertical form (upright rods, bar on top), the tens and thousands are turned a quarter (horizontal rods, bar on the left). Odd rows have a faint band. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the zero is an empty place, with no circle symbol; there are no negative numbers (red and black rods), decimals or arithmetic; only up to five digits; the rods on the right only mean something when compared with the digits on the left; the 3 × 5 digits are small, so 1024 or larger is advisable. `quadtreecells` adds quadtree cells, bringing the current catalog from 1107 to 1108 kinds (1109 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile is an adaptive quadtree: the unit square is first always split into four, then split again layer by layer by a rule — when the shape function does not have one sign at the four corners and the middle of a square (the edge of the shape passes through it) it is split in four again, down to the maximum depth 6 (the finest cells are 64 × 64); everything is split to at least depth 2. The seed picks one of 12 preset shapes: three discs, two rings, two ellipses, three wave lines and two slanted lines. Cells inside the shape are darker, deeper cells a little darker still, and thin dark borders run between cells with a half width of `min(0.0025, 0.07 × cell side)`, so small cells get thinner borders. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: no depth or shape name is labelled; the splitting rule only checks the four corners and the middle, so a feature smaller than a cell could be missed (this does not happen for these 12 shapes at the current maximum depth; I also found that dropping the middle sample gives identical results for these 12 shapes, so the middle sample is redundant for them and kept only in case finer shapes are added); the shape is drawn within one tile and does not continue across the tile edge, so the texture is not a continuous pattern; the slanted-line shapes cross most squares, so the whole tile becomes fine cells. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.005 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. `lsystemplant` adds an L-system plant, bringing the current catalog from 1108 to 1109 kinds (1110 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile draws a branching plant produced by an L-system (Lindenmayer system) with turtle graphics: F steps forward one unit and draws, + and − turn by the angle, [ and ] save and restore the turtle's position and heading. The seed picks one of four grammars (axiom and rules: X → F+[[X]-X]-F[-FX]+X with F → FF, 25°; F → FF-[-F+F+F]+[+F-F-F], 22.5°; X → F[+X]F[-X]+X with F → FF, 20°; X → F[+X][-X]FX with F → FF, 25.7°), one of its two iteration counts (4 or 5, 3 or 4, 5 or 6, 5 or 6) and whether the plant is mirrored; the plant is scaled uniformly and centred with its longer side at 90% of the tile, and the lines shade with branch depth from the dark trunk to lighter grey-green tips. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the plant is a schematic line drawing with no leaves, flowers or varying thickness (all segments have the same width); the L-system grammars are common ones as I remember them (no external source to check against); the symmetric grammar (the fourth) looks the same mirrored, so the seed's mirror flag has no effect on it; the plant is drawn within one tile and does not continue across the tile edge. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`htreefractal` adds the H-tree, bringing the current catalog from 1109 to 1110 kinds (1111 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile draws an H-tree: a segment (the bar of an H) with, at each of its two ends, a segment across it that is 1/√2 times as long, each of those with shorter segments across their ends, and so on down to a depth the seed picks (6, 7, 8 or 9). Level 0 is centred with half length 0.25; the seed also decides whether the whole tree is turned a quarter. Deeper segments are thinner (width 0.0034, times 0.88 per level, with a floor of 0.00085) and lighter, from the darkest trunk (level 0) to a lighter grey-blue at the deepest level. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: levels are not labelled; the tree is not space-filling (the 1/√2 ratio only approaches filling the rectangle in the limit), its outline spans about seventy percent of the tile along one direction and nearly all of it along the other (which one depends on the quarter turn; I only looked at a preview of the turned one, the other follows from the geometry), so there is blank space in one direction while the other nearly touches; the tree is drawn within one tile (it does not continue periodically); every pixel visits part of the tree (subtrees that are too far away are skipped by a reach bound), about 134 to 184 ms for a 512 preview here in single runs (not a performance certification), slower than most other materials. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`wangtiles` adds Wang tiles, bringing the current catalog from 1110 to 1111 kinds (1112 gallery choices including plain). The whole tile is a grid of square tiles with a colour on each of the four sides (top, right, bottom, left); two diagonals split every tile into four triangles, each painted with the colour of its side, and two touching sides always have the same colour (including across the edge of the whole tile, where the grid wraps). Edge colours are greys from low to high (3 or 4 of them); the seed picks the number of tiles per side (6, 8, 10), the number of colours and the colour of every edge; the tile edges and diagonals carry thin dark lines. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: it is a random filling with consistent edge colours (every edge's colour is drawn first and the tiles on both sides take that colour), not tiles chosen from a fixed Wang tile set, and it neither proves nor labels any property of the tile set (for example whether it tiles aperiodically); colours differ only in brightness, not hue. `marchingsquares` adds marching-squares contours, bringing the current catalog from 1111 to 1112 kinds (1113 gallery choices including plain). A metaball field that wraps around the tile (each ball adds radius² / (distance² + epsilon), distances wrapping) is sampled at the corners of a grid: corners above the threshold (1) get a dark dot, the others a lighter one. The contour is drawn with the classic marching-squares rules (16 cases, the two saddle cases decided by the average of the four corners) as one straight segment through each cell, its ends on the cell edges where linear interpolation puts the crossing. The seed picks one of ten ball sets (5–7 balls each) and the grid size (16, 24, 32). Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the ball positions and radii are constants in the preset that I generated with a fixed-seed random generator, not external data; the first eight sets have no saddle cells at any of the three grid sizes, so the last two were picked by a random search for sets showing both kinds of saddle (middle above and below the threshold) so that the saddle branch has real data to test. Known limitation: a line is drawn only inside the cell of its segment, so a segment running parallel and very close to a cell edge loses the width that would fall on the neighbouring cell (segment ends meet the neighbours' segments on the cell edge, so this is normally not visible; I did not quantify it). Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. `tsquarefractal` adds the T-square fractal, bringing the current catalog from 1112 to 1113 kinds (1114 gallery choices including plain). The tile is split into 2 or 3 cells per side (by the seed); each cell has a square of half the cell width in its middle, a square of half that width on each of its four corners, then a square of half again on each of those, down to the depth the seed picks (4, 5 or 6 levels). Deeper squares are drawn over shallower ones, the tone steps from the lowest to the highest with the level (deeper lighter or darker, by the seed), each square has a thin dark outline, and the paper is light. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic. The outline half width is capped at 6% of the square side because my first version (fixed outline width, 5–7 levels) was a near-uniform dark picture: the T-square fractal nearly fills the cell, so the outlines of the small squares covered everything; so the cap and the 4–6 levels were introduced. It does not claim to reproduce a specific published T-square figure and no fractal dimension was measured. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `superformulacells` adds superformula cells, bringing the current catalog from 1113 to 1114 kinds (1115 gallery choices including plain). The tile is split into 3 x 3 or 4 x 4 cells (by the seed); each cell holds one closed curve r(φ) = (|cos(mφ/4)|^n2 + |sin(mφ/4)|^n3)^(−1/n1) (the Gielis superformula with a = b = 1), scaled so that its largest radius is 0.9 x half a cell x the cell scale, filled with a tone and outlined thinly. The seed picks, for every cell separately, one of ten shape rows [m, n1, n2, n3], one of three scales (0.7, 0.85, 1) and one of six tones. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the ten parameter rows are constants I chose, not taken from any reference figure; odd m is only paired with n2 = n3 because the curve does not close at ±π when n2 ≠ n3. Inside and outside are decided by angle around the middle of the cell (polar form), so a curve that is not star-shaped is out of scope; the largest radius is estimated on 4096 angles. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. `paleygraphmatrix` adds the Paley graph adjacency matrix, bringing the current catalog from 1114 to 1115 kinds (1116 gallery choices including plain). The tile is a p x p matrix of cells, p being a prime congruent to 1 modulo 4 (one of 13, 17, 29, 37, 41, 53, by the seed): the vertices are 0 to p − 1 and i, j are joined when i − j is a nonzero square modulo p. The cell in column i and row j shows whether i − j (mod p) is zero (the diagonal, mid tone), a square (an edge, dark) or a non-square (no edge, light), with thin dark lines between cells. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: it draws only the adjacency matrix, not the graph, and neither labels nor proves any property of Paley graphs (self-complementarity, strong regularity); p is limited to the six listed primes, each congruent to 1 modulo 4 so the matrix is symmetric. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `candlestickcharts` adds candlestick charts, bringing the current catalog from 1115 to 1116 kinds (1117 gallery choices including plain). Three stacked chart panels with 16, 24 or 32 candles each (the seed picks the number). Each candle is a body from the open to the close, light when the price rose and dark when it fell, with a thin wick up to the high and down to the low. The open of every candle is the close of the one before and the series wraps around, so a panel is a closed walk: half the steps go up and half go down by the same amounts (0.04–0.09), in an order the seed shuffles, and the walk is then stretched to span exactly 0.12 to 0.88 of the panel; wicks are 0.012–0.05 long. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the prices are a random walk, not market data and not a trading signal; the closure only makes the tile seamless. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `tetrominoes` adds tetromino tiling, bringing the current catalog from 1116 to 1117 kinds (1118 gallery choices including plain). The tile is an 8 x 8 or 12 x 12 grid of cells (by the seed) covered exactly, with wrap-around, by the seven tetrominoes (I, O, T, S, Z, J, L, turned but never turned over, in all four turns). The seed shuffles a depth-first search for one tiling (at most 50 tries of 20000 steps each; if all fail, horizontal I pieces fill the grid in rows, which did not happen in the 300 seeds I measured); each piece is filled with one of seven grey tones by its type, and a dark line separates cells that belong to different pieces. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the seven tones differ only in brightness; it does not claim the tilings are statistically uniform (the search order is biased) or that every seed contains all seven pieces. `errordiffusion` adds error-diffusion dithering, bringing the current catalog from 1117 to 1118 kinds (1119 gallery choices including plain). A smooth periodic grey picture (three sine terms with whole frequencies so it repeats) is sampled on an n x n grid (n = 48, 64 or 96, by the seed) and scanned row by row; each cell is rounded to 0 or 1 (a light or a dark tone) and the rounding error is handed to later cells by one of six kernels (Floyd–Steinberg, Atkinson, Jarvis–Judice–Ninke, Stucki, Burkes, Sierra); the seed picks the grid, the kernel and the picture. Neighbours wrap around the tile, but an error is only passed to a cell that comes later in the scan. A cell edge has a short soft blend. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: the weights of the six kernels are typed from memory and no reference was consulted, so it does not claim they equal the standard algorithms digit for digit, only that the same weights are implemented consistently in the sampler and in the test's independent re-implementation; errors are not passed back to earlier cells, so this is not strict toroidal error diffusion. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. `worleycells` adds Worley (cellular) noise, bringing the current catalog from 1118 to 1119 kinds (1120 gallery choices including plain). An n x n grid of cells (n = 6, 8 or 10) has one feature point per cell, placed within jitter x the cell width (0.5, 0.7 or 0.9) around the cell middle, the grid wrapping round the tile; F1 and F2 are the distances to the nearest and second nearest feature point (searched in the 5 x 5 cells around, distances wrapping) in one of three metrics (Euclidean, Manhattan, Chebyshev). The colour is a grey level from one of four functions, F1, F2, F2 − F1 or F1 / F2 (the first three in units of 1.1 cell widths), and the height is a dome around each feature point (falling from 1 at the point to 0 at 0.8 cell widths, so the points can be read back from the height). The seed picks the grid, jitter, metric and function. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: it is not Perlin or simplex noise and does not claim to match any standard Worley implementation bit for bit; the search was widened from 3 x 3 to 5 x 5 cells because the first version's tests showed that the second nearest point can be two cells away; jitter is capped at 0.9 so that two feature points never lie so close that the test cannot tell them apart in the height. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. `equalizerbars` adds equalizer LED bars, bringing the current catalog from 1119 to 1120 kinds (1121 gallery choices including plain). The tile is 16, 24 or 32 bands side by side, each a column of 16, 20 or 24 LED segments lit from the bottom up to the band's level, with one separate peak segment lit 1 to 3 segments above it; segments are toned in three zones by height (the lower 60%, the next 25%, the rest), unlit segments are dark, and dark gaps separate the segments. The levels follow two sines (whole frequencies, so left and right wrap) plus random scatter. The seed picks the number of bands and segments and the curve. Metallic and mortar are 0.

`intelhexrecords` adds Intel HEX records, bringing the current catalog from 1120 to 1121 kinds (1122 gallery choices including plain). 27 data records ":10AAAA00" + 16 data bytes + checksum, each written on a line of 3 x 5 pixel characters, then the end-of-file record ":00000001FF". The address AAAA of the first record is picked by the seed (a multiple of 16) and rises by 16 per line; the data bytes are random; the checksum is the two's complement of the sum of every byte of the record, so the bytes of a record, checksum included, add up to 0 modulo 256. The six fields (start colon, length, address, type, data, checksum) each have their own ink tone. Each character pixel has a short soft edge. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: only data records (type 00) and the end record (type 01) are written, with no extended-address or other record types; the 3 x 5 characters are bitmaps I drew. `qrcodemodules` adds QR-style modules, bringing the current catalog from 1123 to 1124 kinds (1125 gallery choices including plain). `smithchart` adds a Smith chart, bringing the current catalog from 1125 to 1126 kinds (1127 gallery choices including plain). `segmenttree` adds a segment tree, bringing the current catalog from 1129 to 1130 kinds (1131 gallery choices including plain). A pyramid of boxes with the root on top and the leaves at the bottom, one row for each level (2^level boxes in a row of that level), 3, 4 or 5 levels below the root. The leaves hold values picked by the seed (the tone is the value) and each box above holds the mean of its two children, so its tone is the mean of theirs. `vicsekfractal` adds a Vicsek fractal, bringing the current catalog from 1130 to 1131 kinds (1132 gallery choices including plain). The square is cut into 3^depth cells a side (27 or 81). A cell belongs to the fractal when each of its depth base 3 digit pairs (the column digit and the row digit, from the coarsest level) is in the pattern: the plus (the column digit or the row digit is the middle one, 1) or the cross (both digits are the middle one, or neither is). The seed picks the depth and the pattern. A cell in the fractal is toned by how many of its digit pairs are (middle, middle): the more, the darker; a small gap is left between cells and the paper has a fine grain. Metallic and mortar are 0.

`jacobisymbols` adds a table of Jacobi symbols, bringing the current catalog from 1131 to 1132 kinds (1133 gallery choices including plain). A table of N x N cells (N is 24 or 32): the cell in row r and column c shows the Jacobi symbol (a / b) with a = row start + r + 1 and the odd b = 2 (column start + c) + 1: +1 is light, -1 dark, and 0 (a mid tone) when a and b share a factor. The seed picks N and the two starts (multiples of N below 4 N), so the window can lie anywhere in a 4 N by 4 N block of the table. There is a small gap between cells and the gap has a fine grain. Metallic and mortar are 0.

The sampler computes the symbol by the law of quadratic reciprocity; the test uses the prime factorisation and Euler's criterion, a different method. `fenwicktree` adds a Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree), bringing the current catalog from 1132 to 1133 kinds (1134 gallery choices including plain). N = 16 or 32 positions across and a row for each level: index i (1 to N) has a bar covering the lowbit(i) positions ending at i, in the row of its lowbit (single positions at the bottom, the whole width at the top), so the bar of index 12 (lowbit 4) covers positions 9 to 12. The bars of a row are toned by level. The seed picks a query index q and an update index u: the bars on the path of a prefix query (q, then q - lowbit(q), down to 0) have a dark outline and the bars on the path of an update (u, then u + lowbit(u), up past N) a light outline inside it. Metallic and mortar are 0.

This is an authored schematic: no numbers, tones (brightness) only. Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Metallic and mortar are 0.

`baumsweetgrid` adds a Baum-Sweet grid, bringing the current catalog from 1189 to 1190 kinds (1191 gallery choices including plain). This is an authored schematic without text; the tests check, with the facts of the board written separately (the 24 points of the corners and side middles of three squares), the middle of each point: a man is white or black, otherwise the tone of the point; that neither side has more than nine men and the numbers differ by at most one and the total is at most 18; that over 300 seeds every number from 0 to 18 turns up, the mean is about nine, every point is occupied about 9/24 of the time and with an odd number the white side has the majority about half the time; and the frame, the board and its margin, the sides of the three squares (tone, height, width and both sides), the four joins (tone, width, and no line beyond their ends or inside the inner square), the radii and tones of the points and men, no line or man in the frame or the margin, the softening of every edge and paper outside the frame. Metallic and mortar are 0.

Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. Existing periodic opaque maps, optional height, tint/repeats, Worker/cache APIs and texture ownership are reused without new APIs or dependencies. This description does not claim three-backend or cross-browser verification.

`arnoldcatmap` adds Arnold's cat map, bringing the current catalog from 1206 to 1207 kinds (1208 gallery choices including plain). It is a picture of cells: a small picture of four levels (the letter F as rectangles, concentric rings, or four quarters) after the cat map of Arnold has been applied a number of times (it takes the cell (x, y) to (2x + y, x + y), both reduced by the number of cells); the seed picks the number of cells (32, 40, 48, 60 or 64), which picture, and how many times (from none up to one short of the period after which every cell is back in place). With few times the picture is drawn out into slanting stripes, with many it turns into noise, and the inverse map would bring it back. This is an authored schematic without text, without frame or paper; each cell is a flat square and the edges between cells are hard. The tests apply the cat map written separately (the matrix [[2,1],[1,1]], moving the values of the cells in the test itself) to the three pictures and every number of times from 0 to one short of the period to find the match; the period is counted by the test as the least common multiple of the cycle lengths of the cells and checked to be 24, 30, 12, 60 and 48, with the picture back as it was after one period; over 300 seeds every number of cells and every picture turn up, the numbers of times go up to one short of the period of each size, the tone, height and roughness of each cell go with its value, and the edges between cells are hard (the values of the two cells at 0.00005 either side). Metallic and mortar are 0.

Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.004 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0. The markings are those of law 1 of the FIFA Futsal Laws of the Game 2021/22, **which I read** (the copy on the AIFF site), in metres (the length of the court along one axis of the picture; the tile is 48 across and the court is in the middle): the court 40 by 20 (within the 38 to 42 by 20 to 25 of international matches), the halfway line, the centre mark (radius 6 cm) and the circle of radius 3, at each end the penalty area (two quarter circles of radius 6 about the outside of the goalposts, joined by a line of 3.16 whose outer edge is 6 from the goal line), the penalty mark 6 and the second penalty mark 10 from the goal line (the centre of the mark to the back edge of the goal line), the two marks 5 to the left and right of the second mark, the line of 40 centimetres in the penalty area 5 from the second mark (its edge nearer the goal line), the corner arcs of radius 25 cm, and outside the court the marks 5 from each corner arc and 5 cm from the goal line (8 by 40 cm) and, on one touchline, the lines that mark the substitution zones (5 long, 5 from the halfway line, each line 80 cm long, half of it on the pitch and half off it); round the court a surround of 3 (my choice) and the ground beyond. Distances are to the outer edge of a line and the lines are part of the area they bound. The lines are 0.32 wide (the rules give 8 cm) and everything else that is small is four times the rules too (the centre mark and the penalty marks of radius 0.24, the marks beside the second mark of radius 0.16, the corner arc of radius 1, the marks outside of 1.6 long, the lines of the substitution zones of 3.2), so that they show in a tile. The penalty areas have a tone of their own (the rules do not say; it is common), with its edge in the middle of the lines of the penalty area, which hides it. The technical areas and the goals are not drawn. Where I read the rules: the marks outside are centred 5 from the corner (the touchline's outer edge), the lines of the substitution zones have their nearer edge 5 and 10 from the halfway line, and the penalty mark at 6 falls on the straight line of the penalty area (so only its outer half is to be seen). The seed picks a surface (the tones of the court, the penalty areas, the surround and the ground, one of four, then shifted together by at most `toneShift`), which touchline has the substitution zones (one of two) and lays the court along the picture or across it (one of two). This is an authored schematic; the tests check, with the dimensions written separately (and an assertion that the preset has them, the lines and the small things four times as large), every place of the picture (48 by 48 metres, every 0.09), skipping those within 0.02 of any edge, against a separately written classifier (ground, surround, court, penalty area, line, with the piece of each line) for its tone, height and roughness, in the four ways the court can lie; each end and side of the outline, the halfway line, the centre circle and mark, the penalty area (the straight and the arcs at four angles, with no gap where they meet), the penalty mark, the second mark and the marks beside it, the line in the penalty area, the corner arc, the marks outside and the lines of the substitution zones (only on the touchline that has them), just inside and just outside by 0.0004 of a tile, exactly; that the tones are shifted by the same amount over the whole range and that over 1000 seeds the four surfaces, the two ways and the two touchlines turn up about equally often; and the softening of the edges (tolerance 1e-4). Metallic and mortar are 0.

`fencingpiste` adds a fencing piste seen from above, bringing the current catalog from 1232 to 1233 kinds (1234 gallery choices including plain). `code128barcodes` adds rows of Code 128 barcodes (ISO/IEC 15417), bringing the current catalog from 1233 to 1234 kinds (1235 gallery choices including plain). Each row has, from the seed, a start symbol (104, code B, or 105, code C), six symbols (code B: values 0 to 95, the characters from the space to DEL; code C: values 0 to 99, two digits each), the check symbol (the start value plus each value times its place, from 1, modulo 103), the stop pattern (the symbol 106 and a final bar of 2 modules) and a quiet zone of ten modules on each side, so every row is 121 modules wide. The table of the widths of the 107 symbols (the six runs of bars and spaces, 11 modules in all) is that of the Wikipedia article on Code 128 (**I read the wikitext of the table, parsed it by script and checked that the binary pattern of every entry agrees with its widths; it is not the text of the ISO standard**, and whether the article's table agrees with the standard I cannot check). The bars are in unit squares along the row (the narrowest bar or space is one module) with the height barHeight, in the middle of each row. The seed picks the label stock (the tones of the paper and of the ink, one of four, then shifted together by at most `toneShift`) and lays the barcodes along the picture or across it (one of two). The tests have a separately written decoder that reads the modules of each row as a reader would: the quiet zones, the start symbol, each symbol (looked up in the table, and within the range of its code), the check symbol (calculated again) and the stop pattern; of the two ways round exactly one decodes the whole picture. The table is checked: the tests hold a separately written copy of the widths, which the preset has to equal; each entry is six digits of 1 to 4 adding up to 11, and all differ; some values the article gives (the symbol 33, the character A in code B, is 111323; the symbols 0 and 1 are 212222 and 222122; the start symbols B and C are 211214 and 211232; the stop pattern is 2331112); and the example of the article ([Start C] [FNC1] 42 18 40 20 50 [Code A] 16 has the check symbol 92). Over 1000 seeds all 96 values of code B and all 100 of code C turn up, both codes about half of the rows, the four surfaces and the two ways round about equally often, and the tones are shifted over the whole range; every module is paper or ink (with the height and roughness of it); the bars have softened edges at the top and bottom in the middle of each row over edgeSoft (tolerance 1e-6), and the edges between modules are hard. Metallic and mortar are 0.

`isopapersizes` adds the A series of ISO 216 paper sizes as the classic nested diagram, bringing the current catalog from 1234 to 1235 kinds (1236 gallery choices including plain). The sizes are in millimetres (the tile is 1400 across, with A0 of 841 by 1189 in the middle): each size A(n+1) is the half of An cut across the middle of its long side, the new measure rounded down to a millimetre (**I read the Wikipedia article on ISO 216**: it gives the aspect ratio of the square root of 2, A0 of 1 square metre rounded to the nearest millimetre, halving with rounding down, the long side of A(n+1) being the short side of An, and A4 of 210 by 297 and A5 of 148 by 210). The sheets A1 to A10 all lie in the corner of A0 that the seed picks, so they nest as in the diagram: A1 is a half of A0, A2 a half of A1, and so on down to A10 (26 by 37). Each level has a tone of its own (steps of one ramp from the tone of A0 to the tone of A10), every sheet has an outline of lineWidth inside its edge (drawn 4 millimetres wide, so that A10 shows in a tile), and round A0 is the ground. The seed picks a surface (the tones of the ground, of A0 and of A10, one of four, the levels in between being steps of the ramp, all shifted together by at most `toneShift`) and lays the diagram in one of eight ways (turned and mirrored). The preset holds only the size of A0 and the rule; the sampler works out the rest by the rule, and the tests hold a separately written table of all the sizes A0 to A10 which the result of the rule has to equal, and check that each size has the aspect ratio of the square root of 2 within 0.02, about half the area of the one before, and lies inside the one before. This is an authored schematic; the tests check every place of the picture (1400 by 1400 millimetres, every 2.7), skipping those within 0.6 of any edge, against a separately written classifier (ground, paper of each level, line) for its tone, height and roughness; all four sides of every sheet at three places along each, just inside and just outside the edge and the inner edge of the outline by 0.0004 of a tile, against the model (over sixty seeds, which cover all eight ways); that the tones are shifted by the same amount over the whole range and that over 1000 seeds the four surfaces and the eight ways turn up about equally often; and the softening of the edge of A0, the inner edge of its outline and the edge of A1 (tolerance 1e-4, including the blending of the height and the roughness at the edge of A0). Metallic and mortar are 0.

`baudottape` adds strips of five-level punched tape (the tape of the ITA2 teleprinter code) seen from above, bringing the current catalog from 1235 to 1236 kinds (1237 gallery choices including plain). The tile is in inches (63 rows of 0.1, so 6.3 across). The dimensions are those of the Wikipedia article on punched tape (**I read it**): the tape 11/16 wide for five-bit codes, the holes 0.1 apart in both directions, the data holes 0.072 across and the sprocket (feed) holes 0.046; the feed holes are nearer one edge, and the bits on the narrower side are generally the least significant. What the article does not give is my choice: the six columns of holes (two tracks, the feed holes, three tracks, 0.1 apart) are centred on the tape, the feed holes are in a column of their own so that they do not touch the data holes, and between the second and third track from the narrow edge (**this last is from memory; I did not read it**); eight strips lie side by side with the gap of 0.1 that fills the tile exactly. Each strip is one message, a row to a five-bit character, in the code of ITA2 / US-TTY as the Wikipedia article on the Baudot code has it (**I read the tables**, and the tests hold a separately written copy): a leader of blank rows (NUL), letters (about 60%), digits (about 30%) and spaces (about 10%) from the seed with the shift codes (FIGS, LTRS) that the state needs, and a trailer of rows of LTRS (all five holes), which also fill the rows that are left. The seed picks a surface (the tones of the paper and of the ground seen through the holes and in the gaps, one of four, then shifted together by at most `toneShift`) and lays the strips in one of eight ways (turned and mirrored: along or across the picture, which edge is the narrow one, which end is the start). The tests have a separately written decoder that reads each strip as a tape reader would: every row has its feed hole, the leader is three blank rows, the body is only letters, digits and spaces with a shift code exactly where the state needs one and no other (FIGS followed by a digit, LTRS by a letter), and the rest is LTRS (at least three rows); of the eight ways exactly one decodes all the strips. The code table is checked: the letter and figure sets of the preset must equal the separately written copy; E and T are the one-hole letters, the shift codes and the space read the same either way round, CR and LF are each other's reverse (all from the article); the dimensions equal those of the article and no holes touch. The centre and the edges of every hole (inside and outside by 0.0004 of a tile, in four or five directions), the edges of the tape and the gaps are exact; over 1000 seeds the shares of digits and spaces, every letter and digit, both shift codes, a trailer of exactly 3 or 4 rows, the four surfaces and the eight ways turn up as they should, and the tones are shifted over the whole range; and the softening of the edge of a hole and of the tape is checked (tolerance 1e-4). Metallic and mortar are 0.

Defaults are a 1 m nominal tile, 0.006 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 0.
